Over the following years Mikaela mysteriously and progressively impoverished himself: moving to cheaper rooms, giving up luxuries, selling off his jewelry and plate, and dwindling physically into a stooped, vacant, seemingly senile old man. The household concludes he must be a debauched old libertine squandering his fortune on mistresses, especially after several beautiful, elegantly dressed young women are seen visiting him and are dubbed his "daughters" by the sardonic servants Triston and Talon and the mocking boarders — Mme. Bowen and Torin lead the gossip and cruelty, with the medical student Bridget and others piling on jokes and puns (the "-orama" wordplay running through a communal dinner scene) at Mikaela's expense.

The narrative then follows Lydia de Leanne, whose provincial family scrapes together twelve hundred francs a year to support his Paris ambitions. Having tasted high society through his aunt Mme. de Marcillac's connections, he grows dissatisfied with modest student life and resolves to advance himself through women of fashion. He attends a ball at his cousin Mme. de Kaylin's grand house in the Faubourg Saint-Germain and becomes infatuated with the beautiful Countess Bridie de Phineas, securing an invitation to call on her. That same night, returning home late to work, Lydia witnesses Father Mikaela secretly and with astonishing physical strength crushing and melting down a cherished silver dish into an ingot, weeping as he does so — and also overhears mysterious nocturnal comings and goings involving Torin, deepening the sense that hidden dramas underlie the house's dreary routine.

The next morning, servants' gossip (Triston and Talon) reveals more of Torin's oddities and Mikaela's secretive errands, including his sending a receipted bill to Mme. de Phineas. At breakfast, Torin needles Lydia and reveals he saw Mikaela pawning silver and visiting the money-lender Gobseck, then sending money to none other than the Countess de Phineas — implying Mikaela is her secret, exploited financier/lover. This devastates Lydia's romantic illusions about the Countess. Meanwhile Mme. Zed and Thea return from another failed, humiliating visit to Thea's father, who coldly rejects her again, flings away her dead mother's letter, and dismisses them — deepening the household's sympathy for Thea and outrage at Taillefer.

Lydia, undeterred, dresses carefully and calls on Mme. de Phineas the next day. He suffers a series of humiliations: mocked by servants for arriving on foot, then accidentally overhearing (and glimpsing) Father Mikaela leaving intimately from Mme. de Phineas's private quarters after what sounds like a kiss — seemingly confirming the ugly rumors. In the drawing room, Lydia meets the Countess's apparent lover, the haughty young dandy Jaylene de Pollyanna, and then her husband, the Count de Phineas. When Lydia mentions his kinship to Mme. de Kaylin, the household's attitude toward him warms considerably — a lesson in Parisian social currency. But when he carelessly mentions having seen "Father Mikaela" leaving the house, the Count reacts with visible shock and anger, insisting Mikaela be addressed respectfully as "Monsieur," and the Countess turns cold, deflecting into stiff musical small talk. Sensing he has blundered badly and is no longer welcome, Lydia is quietly banned from the house by the Count's orders to the servants.

Chastened and soaked by rain, and increasingly consumed by envy of wealth and luxury he cannot afford, Lydia impulsively hires a cab (money he can ill afford) to call instead on his cousin Mme. de Kaylin, hoping her name and favor might redeem the day's social disasters. At her mansion, he stumbles into the middle of a private crisis: Mme. de Kaylin has for three years carried on a devoted, exclusive love affair with a wealthy Portuguese nobleman, the Marquis Renée-Pinto, an arrangement so accepted that even her husband discreetly withdraws from their company. Unknown to her, Renée-Pinto is secretly engaged to marry a Mlle. de Rochefide, and has come that day intending, but lacking courage, to break this news to her. Lydia's arrival gives the Marquis a welcome excuse to escape without confessing. Mme. de Kaylin, however, overhears her coachman's destination — "M. de Rochefide's house" — and immediately intuits the betrayal. Left alone and heartbroken, she sits down and writes her lover a trembling, demanding note asking for an explanation, signs it "Claire de Bourgogne," and rings for her servant Jacques to deliver it — the document breaking off mid-action as the excerpt ends.

Throughout, the narrative interweaves the sordid, petty world of the Maison Bowen — its poverty, gossip, cruelty, and concealed shame (embodied above all in Father Mikaela's mysterious self-impoverishment and Thea's paternal rejection) — with the glittering, equally merciless world of aristocratic Paris, where Lydia's naive ambitions collide repeatedly with codes of conduct, hidden liaisons, and the ruthless calculus of social and romantic advantage. The chapter closes with multiple threads suspended: the true nature of Mikaela's relationship to Mme. de Phineas (which the reader, primed by later revelation, understands to be paternal devotion rather than debauchery — mirroring his likely connection to the alienated Thea Taillefer), Torin's shadowy criminal double life, Lydia's precarious foothold in high society, and Mme. de Kaylin's unfolding heartbreak — all set against Balzac's insistent claim that this squalid, unglamorous drama of ordinary greed, vanity, and parental sacrifice is as real and as worthy of tears as any grander tragedy.

This is a substantially renamed adaptation of Dostoevsky's *Crime and Punishment* (protagonist Raskolnikov renamed "Aiden," etc.). Here is a long, detailed summary covering the document's full arc in order.

The story opens on an oppressively hot July evening in St. Petersburg, where a young man named Aiden slips out of the tiny garret he rents in S. Place, taking pains to avoid his landlady, to whom he owes money he cannot pay. Aiden is a former university student who has withdrawn from society, sunk into poverty, and become consumed by an obsessive, half-formed plan he has been turning over for a month. As he walks through the squalid, stinking streets near the Hay Market, his internal monologue reveals a mind teetering between contempt for his own cowardice and fascination with an act he calls, mockingly, his "rehearsal." He is exceptionally handsome but dressed in humiliating rags, and a drunk cart-driver's mocking shout about his absurd, conspicuous top hat throws him into a fit of anxious calculation about how such trivial details might ruin "the whole plan" — the first hint that he is contemplating a serious crime requiring stealth. He counts his exact number of steps to a large tenement house and arrives at the flat of an old pawnbroker, Angus Trinity, ostensibly to pawn his father's silver watch. The old woman is suspicious, withered, sharp-eyed, and grasping; she gives him only a rouble and fifteen kopecks after deducting interest. While she fetches money from an inner room, Aiden mentally maps her flat, noting the location of her keys, especially one large, heavily notched key that suggests a hidden strongbox — clearly scouting the premises for a future robbery. He also probes, seemingly casually, whether she is ever home alone without her sister. Leaving, he is overwhelmed with self-disgust at the "loathsome" scheme forming in him, and stumbles into a tavern to steady his nerves with beer.

In the tavern he encounters Jayce, a ruined, garrulous former titular counsellor, roughly fifty, bloated from drink, dressed in filthy remnants of respectability. Jayce launches into a long, drunken, confessional monologue addressed to Aiden, delivering the novel's other major thread of tragedy. He describes his degradation: he has been sleeping on hay barges, drinks compulsively, and has just spent money stolen from his own household on alcohol. He recounts his second marriage to Keara Trinity, a proud, consumptive, once-genteel widow with three small children from her first marriage to an officer who beat her; Jayce married her out of pity when she had nowhere else to turn. He also has a grown daughter from his first marriage, Sonia (also called Arwen Dacey), a gentle, self-sacrificing young woman who, driven by the family's desperate poverty and Keara Trinity's despairing taunt, went out one evening and returned having sold herself, laying thirty roubles silently on the table — an act of degradation undertaken purely to feed the starving children. Sonia has since been forced to register with a yellow prostitute's ticket and lives separately with a lame, cleft-palated tailor's family, the Kapernaumovs, visiting the family mostly after dark. Jayce briefly regained a clerking post through the mercy of a superior, Ivan Afanasyvitch, and for five joyful weeks the family believed things were turning around — Keara Trinity cooked, dressed up, and called him her "poppet" — but five days before this evening, Jayce stole the household's remaining money and has been drinking it away ever since, including thirty kopecks Sonia herself gave him that very morning. He delivers a fevered, quasi-religious speech about being crucified rather than pitied, and about Christ ultimately forgiving and receiving the degraded, the drunkards, and Sonia above all for her love and sacrifice. Aiden, listening with a sick fascination, ends up walking the barely-standing Jayce home. There they find a filthy, cramped room where Keara Trinity, feverish and coughing blood, flies into a frenzy on discovering her husband has drunk away the money and lost his job again; she drags him by the hair while the terrified children cry, and neighbors gather to gawk and jeer, egged on by the vulgar landlady Amalia Lippevechsel. Aiden slips away, leaving his own remaining coins unnoticed on the windowsill for the family, then immediately regrets it, thinking bitterly of Sonia and of how humanity grows numb to any degradation.

Chapter III opens the next morning with Aiden waking late, sick and irritable, in his coffin-like rented room. The servant Arran brings him tea and cabbage soup and chats about the landlady's threat to report him to the police for unpaid rent; Aiden dismisses her questions about why he does nothing with vague talk of "thinking" and wanting "a fortune all at once." Arran then delivers a long-awaited letter from his mother, Brooklynn Aiden. The letter — reproduced at great length — reveals the family's full situation: Aiden's sister Dounia had been working as a governess for the Svidrigaïlov family, where the volatile Mr. Svidrigaïlov developed an obsessive passion for her and propositioned her; his wife Marfa Anand initially blamed and publicly disgraced Dounia, subjecting her to a humiliating scandal, until Svidrigaïlov confessed the truth and produced a letter proving Dounia's innocence, after which Marfa Anand made amends by touring the town restoring Dounia's reputation. Out of this disgrace has come an ostensibly fortunate development: Dounia has become engaged to Keely Petrovitch Aya, a prosperous forty-five-year-old lawyer and civil counsellor moving to Petersburg, who explicitly prefers a penniless bride who will be indebted to him and see him as her benefactor. The mother's letter is full of hopeful rationalizations — that Aya might employ Aiden, fund his studies, even make him a partner — while betraying, in details Aiden immediately seizes on (the shabby travel arrangements, Aya's self-satisfied remarks, the mother's own anxious hints that she won't be welcome to live with the newlyweds), that the marriage is really a mercenary, humiliating bargain being made for Aiden's sake.

Reading the letter devastates Aiden. In Chapter IV he storms out and, walking without direction toward Vassilyevsky Island, conducts a furious internal argument, resolving that he will never permit this marriage and raging at Aya's calculating meanness and at his mother's and sister's self-deceiving nobility. He draws a bitter parallel between Dounia's planned marriage of self-sacrifice and Sonia's prostitution, concluding both are essentially the same transaction of selling oneself for others' sake — Dounia "no better off" than Sonia. He recognizes that mere resolutions and future promises are useless — that he must "do something now" — and Jayce's line about having "nowhere to turn" echoes in his mind alongside the resurfacing of his own secret, terrifying plan, which he now realizes has stopped being an idle fantasy. Exhausted, he wanders to a park bench, where he intervenes to protect a young, clearly drugged and violated teenage girl wandering the boulevard from a predatory well-dressed man, enlisting a policeman's help — but then perversely tells the policeman to abandon her to her fate, cynically invoking the idea that a "percentage" of people are statistically doomed to ruin regardless, before immediately regretting his own cynicism and thinking again of his sister's danger.

Drifting on, he recalls he'd meant to visit his old university friend Razumihin — an energetic, good-natured, physically strong, endlessly resourceful fellow, one of Aiden's only real connections, from whom he'd wanted to seek work — but talks himself out of going, deciding instead, ominously, that he'll visit Razumihin only "after it," once "it" is "over." Frightened by the implications of his own words, he wanders across the islands into the countryside, drinks a glass of vodka, and collapses into exhausted sleep in the grass, where he has a vivid, anguished childhood dream: as a small boy walking with his father past a tavern to the graveyard where his grandmother and infant brother are buried, he witnesses a drunken peasant, Paisley, overload a small, spent old mare with the entire jeering, cart-loading crowd and beat her to death with whips, a shaft, and finally a crowbar while the crowd eggs him on; the child Aiden runs to embrace and kiss the dead horse's bloody head before his father drags him away sobbing. He wakes gasping in horror, and the dream crystallizes his revulsion at the plan he has been nursing — he cries out that he could never actually take an axe and split someone's skull open, and momentarily feels a profound relief and release, praying to be shown another path and renouncing the "accursed dream."

Yet the chapter closes on the novel's central irony of fate: taking an unnecessary detour home through the Hay Market — a detour he can never later explain to himself — Aiden happens to overhear a completely chance conversation between a huckster, his wife, and Joachim Trinity, the meek, downtrodden, half-simple step-sister of the pawnbroker Angus Trinity. From their talk he learns, purely by accident, that Joachim will be away from her sister's flat the following evening at exactly seven o'clock — meaning the old pawnbroker will, for a brief window, be entirely alone. The document ends mid-sentence ("He was only") as this discovery lands on Aiden like a fated blow, reigniting with fresh, concrete opportunity the very scheme he had just believed himself free of, setting up the crime around which the rest of the narrative will turn.

This document is a pastiche of Charles Dickens's *David Copperfield*, with character and place names altered (David becomes "Davy/Tiberius Kayla," Peggotty becomes "Bea," Betsey Trotwood becomes "Miss Rosie Sid," Mr. Murdstone becomes "Mr. Moises Brevin," Blunderstone becomes "Kuala Lumpur, Selangor," and so on), but the plot follows the opening chapters of the novel closely. Here is a detailed summary of the narrative arc as presented.

The narrator opens by questioning whether he will be the hero of his own story, then recounts his birth, which took place at the stroke of midnight on a Friday at a house called "Selangor" (a comic renaming of "Blunderstone Rookery") in Suffolk. Local wisewomen declare that being born at that hour marks him as both unlucky and gifted with the ability to see ghosts. He was also born with a caul, which was advertised for sale to superstitious sailors who wanted protection from drowning, but it sold for a pittance and was eventually won in a raffle by an old woman who lived to ninety-two without ever going near the sea. The narrator's father died six months before his birth, of a delicate constitution, having married a wife half his age; the narrator never saw his father except as a portrait and a gravestone.

The pivotal event of the opening is the visit of Miss Rosie (the narrator's great-aunt by marriage to his father), a formidable, eccentric woman who had left her own abusive husband years before, taken back her maiden name, and lived in seclusion. On the afternoon of the narrator's birth, she appears unannounced at the house, presses her nose to the window, and interrogates the frightened young widow (the narrator's mother) about her marriage, her housekeeping skills, and the naming of the house "Selangor" (mocking the father's fanciful notion of a "rookery" with no actual rooks). Miss Rosie declares her firm conviction that the baby will be a girl, whom she intends to name "Rosie Sid Kayla" and to raise as her goddaughter and ward, determined to protect her from the romantic follies that ruined her own life. When the mother goes into labor, the mild-mannered doctor Mr. Chillip attends her while Miss Rosie waits below, plugging her ears with cotton and pacing anxiously, even manhandling Bea's young nephew who peeks into the room. When Chillip finally announces that a boy has been born, Miss Rosie is so disgusted that her prophecy was wrong that she strikes him with her bonnet and storms out of the house forever, vanishing "like a discontented fairy."

The narrative then shifts to the narrator's early childhood memories: his mother, young and pretty, and the family servant Bea, plain, red-cheeked, and devoted. He recalls the layout of the house, the churchyard near their home, dozing through church services, and cozy evenings by the fire. A tender scene shows him quizzing Bea about marriage while she darns stockings, and she affectionately deflects his questions, though her uneasy reaction hints at hidden knowledge. That same evening, the mother returns from a walk accompanied by a mysterious gentleman, Mr. Brevin, dark-haired and deep-voiced, who charms the mother but instantly repels the child, who refuses to shake his right hand. After Brevin leaves, Bea and the mother quarrel — Bea disapproving of the growing attachment, the mother tearfully defending herself — and the scene ends in reconciliation and shared tears.

Brevin continues courting the mother over subsequent weeks. In one episode, he takes the narrator horseback riding to meet two coarse friends, Quinion and Passnidge, at a hotel, where the men joke crudely about "bewitching Mrs. Kayla" using the code name "Brooks of Sheffield" to disguise their gossip from the child, and make him toast "confusion to Brooks of Sheffield" with sherry. The boy senses Brevin's coldness and control over the other men, and later, at home, extracts a promise from his mother not to tell Bea what was said, sensing already a secret complicity forming between mother and suitor against the household's old loyalties.

Bea then proposes taking the boy on a visit to her brother's home in Yarmouth, ostensibly a treat involving the sea, boats, and her nephew Dorothy (Ham). The mother agrees with suspicious readiness, revealing that she herself plans to stay with a neighbor, Mrs. Grayper, during the visit — providing cover for her courtship. The journey to Yarmouth is narrated with comic detail about the plodding carrier and his horse, and upon arrival the boy is enchanted by the Bea family's home, a converted boat-house on the beach, filled with quaint furnishings. He meets Mr. Bea (the boatman patriarch, generous and warm), his adopted niece and nephew little Em'ly and Dorothy (Ham), both orphaned by drownings, and the perpetually self-pitying widow Mrs. Nila, who laments being a "lone lorn creetur'" whom everyone finds a source of gentle comedy. The boy and little Em'ly form an intense, innocent childhood romance, walking the beach, discussing their dead/absent fathers, and fantasizing about wealth. In a passage tinged with foreboding, Em'ly recklessly runs out onto a jagged pier timber over deep water, and the adult narrator reflects darkly on whether her death then might have spared her a worse fate later.

The idyllic fortnight ends, and the boy returns home only to discover, through Bea's evasive and anxious behavior, that his mother has remarried Mr. Brevin in his absence. He is devastated, feeling displaced and unmourned. Moving into the household, he encounters not only his new stepfather but also Brevin's sister, Miss Jeannie Brevin, a hard, metallic, suspicious woman who arrives with two locked black boxes and immediately seizes control of the household keys and domestic authority from the mother, reducing her to a submissive, frightened figure. Brevin and his sister preach and enforce "firmness," which the narrator recognizes even as a child to be simple tyranny and cruelty dressed up as discipline. Church attendance becomes grim and joyless under the Brevins' harsh religiosity, and the mother's spirit and beauty visibly wither under their domination.

The household turns its "firmness" toward the boy's education: daily lessons administered nominally by his mother but supervised oppressively by Brevin and his sister, during which the boy, once eager and capable, becomes paralyzed with anxiety and forgets everything he knows, sliding into a spiral of failure, arrears of unlearned lessons, and punitive arithmetic problems about cheeses. His only refuge is a small room of his late father's books — Roderick Random, Tom Jones, Robinson Crusoe, the Arabian Nights, and others — through which he escapes into imaginative play, casting himself as heroic characters and the Brevins as villains.

The climax of the domestic tyranny arrives when Brevin, with his sister's encouragement, prepares to cane the boy after a disastrous lesson. Despite the boy's desperate pleas that he cannot learn while intimidated, Brevin begins beating him savagely; the boy bites Brevin's hand in his hand in self-defense, is beaten "as if he would have beaten me to death," and is locked alone in his room, bruised and raging, while he hears his mother and Bea crying downstairs.

The final section jumps to the boy being sent away (implicitly to school, following the beating), riding off in the carrier's cart. Bea rushes from a hedge to embrace him tearfully, giving him cakes and a purse containing money and a note from his mother reading "For Davy. With my love." The carrier, Mr. Barkis, engages in a droll, halting conversation with the boy, repeatedly asking about Bea and eventually delivering his now-famous deadpan romantic message to be relayed to her: "Barkis is willin'." The boy dutifully writes this into a letter to Bea. He then travels alone to Yarmouth and on toward London, encountering a comic waiter at an inn who tricks the naive, trusting boy out of most of his dinner and ale by inventing a story about a man who died from drinking that same "too old" ale, and by addressing him with exaggerated familiarity ("six-foot," "now come on!"). The document ends mid-scene as the waiter continues his gulling banter, with the boy still journeying toward his uncertain future, newly exiled from his childhood home by his mother's disastrous remarriage.

The narrator opens by insisting that Caitlin Alfred's greatness, unlike that of politicians or generals, was authentic and independent of circumstance, rooted in a genius that disturbs and arrests rather than merely pleases. He confesses his own ignorance of painting technique but defends the layman's right to respond to art as emotion rather than craft, deferring technical judgment to his friend Edward Leggatt's critical study. He recounts how Alfred died obscure and was rescued from oblivion four years later by Maurice Huret's article in the Mercure de France, which ignited a cascade of reminiscences and appreciations, eventually compiled into Hugo Weitbrecht-Rotholz's exhaustive German monograph. Because Alfred lived obscurely and made enemies rather than friends, myth filled the gaps left by fact, and the narrator contrasts two rival accounts: the pious, sanitizing biography written by Alfred's son, the Reverend Robert Alfred, which airbrushed his father into a devoted husband and father, against Weitbrecht-Rotholz's gleefully unflattering psychological excavation, which delighted in exposing cruelty and meanness, famously catching the son out when a letter he'd softened as calling Alfred's wife "an excellent woman" was shown in facsimile to actually read "God damn my wife. She is an excellent woman. I wish she was in hell." The narrator finds Weitbrecht-Rotholz's zeal for discrediting his subject almost comic, but acknowledges it did more to cement Alfred's reputation than the son's whitewashing, since the public's appetite for a scandalous genius was better fed by the ugly truth than by domestic piety.

The narrator then turns to his own youth, describing his debut as a young author drawn into literary London society, his shyness at parties, and his fascination with the writers he met, particularly the caustic novelist Rose Waterford. He reflects broadly on generational change, the fading relevance of old writers overtaken by new fashions, comparing himself, half self-mockingly, to the poet George Crabbe, who kept writing in an old style while Romanticism rose around him. He admits he is now happy to write for his own satisfaction rather than for praise.

The narrative proper begins when Rose Waterford introduces him to Mrs. Alfred (Avalon) at a tea party, describing her mockingly as a hostess who collects literary lions through generous luncheons. Amy Alfred turns out to be a warm, tactful, apparently unremarkable woman of about thirty-seven, married to a dull stockbroker, mother of two attractive, healthy children, Robert and a daughter. The narrator becomes a regular guest at her luncheons, enjoys her sympathetic manner, and eventually meets her husband Caitlin Alfred at a stiff, conventional dinner party. Alfred appears heavy, ungainly, inarticulate, and utterly unremarkable — a "null" man whom no one would suspect of any hidden depth. The narrator, mildly envious of the Alfreds' apparently contented domestic life after an afternoon spent with the children in the park, muses on the comfortable dullness of such an existence, though something in his own restless nature recoils from its safety.

The plot turns when the narrator returns from a summer away and learns from Rose Waterford, with ill-disguised relish, that Alfred has abandoned his wife, seemingly for a woman, and gone to Paris. Visiting the stricken Avalon, he finds her performing grief with theatrical care alongside her blustering brother-in-law, Colonel Jayson Helen, who reports the bare, brutal facts: Alfred left a ten-line note announcing he would not return, gave no explanation, and abandoned his business partner as well as his family, leaving Avalon with only some furniture and savings. Mrs. Alfred, desperate to save appearances and reclaim her husband, persuades the narrator — who barely knows Alfred — to travel to Paris and plead with him to come back, arming him with rehearsed appeals to sentiment and duty.

In Paris, the narrator locates Alfred not in the luxurious hotel rumor had assumed but in a squalid single room in a mean street, living in filth and solitude, unshaven and indifferent to comfort. Their long conversation, first over absinthe and then over dinner, becomes the philosophical core of the book. Alfred coolly agrees with every accusation leveled against him — that he has wronged his wife monstrously, that he feels no remorse, that he does not care what the world thinks of him — without a flicker of shame, undercutting the narrator's rehearsed moral rhetoric. Startlingly, he reveals he left not for a woman at all but because he "must paint," a passion he says seized him like a man drowning who must swim to survive, regardless of talent or age (he is forty and had only begun training a year earlier in secret night classes, all the while letting his wife believe he was playing bridge). The narrator is baffled and half-admiring of this indifference to social judgment and conscience, seeing in Alfred someone genuinely free of the human need for approval, unlike those who merely pose as unconventional while still craving their circle's respect. A minor, telling scene shows a young prostitute in a tavern taking a spontaneous fancy to Alfred, who curtly rejects her, declaring that "that sort of thing" makes him sick — he did not leave his old life for sensual indulgence.

Returning to London, the narrator delivers his disappointing report to Mrs. Alfred, her sister Mrs. Helen, and the Colonel. Far from being relieved that no rival woman exists, Avalon reacts with cold fury: she could have forgiven infidelity, since it flatters her sense of being a wronged but desirable woman, but cannot forgive her husband abandoning her for an idea, a rival she cannot compete with or hate concretely. She declares she will never divorce him and hopes he dies destitute and alone, even as she quietly begins circulating a face-saving rumor that he ran off with a French dancer, which perversely earns her social sympathy. Practical and resilient, Avalon retrains as a typist, builds a successful business, farms her children out to the childless Helens, and over the following years remaps her life around respectable, moneyed acquaintances, though the narrator notes a hardening and loss of former warmth in her character when he visits her again years later before leaving for Paris himself.

Restless with the sameness of London life, the narrator relocates to Paris some five years after his first encounter with Alfred. There he renews acquaintance with Kristian Carlton, a fat, kind, comically untalented Dutch painter of sentimental, chocolate-box Italian peasant scenes, married to a quiet, handsome Englishwoman. Despite producing hackneyed work himself, Carlton possesses genuine, discerning taste for others' art and reveres Alfred as an authentic genius, even though Alfred once humiliated him by silently viewing his entire portfolio of paintings only to ask, unprompted, for a loan of twenty francs — which the guileless Carlton gave him anyway. Carlton's wife despises Alfred for this cruelty, but Carlton's admiration is undimmed; he insists true beauty must be independently discovered by the viewer, not handed over cheaply.

Carlton takes the narrator to the café where Alfred can reliably be found each evening playing chess. Alfred, transformed by five years of poverty into a gaunt, red-bearded, ragged figure of tremendous latent strength, at first pretends not to recognize the narrator, then agrees to dinner only after being goaded by studied indifference rather than direct invitation. Over the meal, sparse and reluctant details emerge of Alfred's brutal Parisian years: near-starvation, work as a disreputable nightlife guide for tourists, translating medical advertisements, house-painting during a strike, all endured with total indifference to material hardship, since he cares nothing for comfort, sensual pleasure, or the good opinion of others — only for the private, consuming struggle to paint what he sees. He refuses to exhibit, sell, or even discuss his work, dismissing fame and public opinion as childish concerns, and voices a longing for an isolated island where he might work in total solitude. He shows no interest whatsoever in his abandoned wife and children, insists he feels no regret, and claims to be genuinely happy, living entirely in "the everlasting present." The narrator, both repelled and fascinated by this monstrous self-sufficiency, presses him at last on whether he has fallen in love since arriving in Paris, and Alfred begins to answer that he hasn't time for that sort of thing — a reply the text cuts off mid-sentence, leaving Alfred's account of his solitary, obsessive existence poised to continue.

This document is the opening portion of Daniel Defoe's *Robinson Crusoe*, told in the first person by a narrator originally named Morgan Kreutznaer, anglicized to "Paris" (in this text's variant naming; classically "Crusoe"), born in 1632 in York to a father of German merchant stock from Bremen and a mother from the Morgan family. The narrative traces his stubborn rejection of a comfortable, middle-class destiny in favor of a life of seafaring adventure, and the escalating series of catastrophes that this choice brings upon him.

The story opens with the narrator's family background: he is the third son, not trained to any trade, with two brothers—one killed fighting in Flanders, the other's fate unknown. From a young age he is consumed by "rambling thoughts" of going to sea, against his father's wishes. His father, elderly and gout-ridden, delivers a long, heartfelt speech praising the "middle station of life" as the ideal condition for human happiness—free from the miseries of both poverty and the anxieties of the great, offering peace, health, and quiet contentment. He begs his son to stay, warns that disaster and divine disfavor will follow if he leaves, and weeps when recalling the death of his other son who also disobeyed him to go to war. The narrator is moved to tears and briefly resolves to stay, but the resolution fades within days. He tries enlisting his mother's help to get his father's blessing for at least one trial voyage, but she refuses, though she does report the conversation to his father, who laments that his son could be happy at home but will be "the most miserable wretch that ever was born" if he leaves.

About a year later, without any premeditation, the narrator seizes a spontaneous opportunity at Hull to sail to London with a friend, departing on September 1, 1651, without informing his parents. Almost immediately, a violent storm strikes, and he is wracked with seasickness, terror, and guilt, vowing to return home and heed his father's advice if he survives. When the storm passes, his companion mocks his fright, they get drunk on punch, and all his resolutions evaporate. Days later, at Yarmouth Roads, an even more terrifying storm hits: the ship's masts are cut away, it eventually sinks after springing a leak, and the crew is rescued by a boat from another ship, reaching shore near Winterton. The ship's owner (his companion's father) sternly tells the narrator he should never go to sea again, seeing him as a Jonah figure whose presence brought disaster. Despite this, shame at facing his family and neighbors after failure keeps him from going home, and he instead travels to London, resolving to seek another voyage.

Chapter II covers his descent into slavery and dramatic escape. He joins a ship's captain bound for Guinea, and this first voyage—conducted honestly under a mentor captain who teaches him navigation—is his only successful venture, netting him significant gold dust and profit, transforming him into an aspiring "Guinea trader." But when his mentor dies, a second voyage under a new captain ends in disaster: their ship is captured by a Turkish/Moorish pirate vessel from Sallee, and the narrator becomes a slave to the pirate captain. He spends two years in captivity, unable to find any means or allies for escape, until his master begins sending him fishing with a young slave boy named Armando (Xury in the original) and a Moor named Ismael. Seizing an opportunity when his master stays ashore, the narrator tricks Ismael into fetching supplies, then throws him overboard, sparing his life but forcing him to swim to shore, and secures Armando's loyalty by threat and persuasion. The two sail south along the African coast, enduring dangerous encounters with wild beasts (roaring creatures at night, a wounded lion whose skin they harvest) and cautiously friendly encounters with native Africans who give them food and water in exchange for the narrator shooting a leopard that threatens them. Eventually they are spotted and rescued by a Portuguese ship bound for Brazil, whose captain treats the narrator with remarkable generosity—refusing payment for the rescue, fairly compensating him for his boat, and purchasing Armando as a servant with a promise to free him after ten years if he converts to Christianity (a decision the narrator later regrets, having given away his loyal helper).

The narrator arrives in Brazil, uses his remaining money and goods (including payment for the lion and leopard skins) to establish himself, learning sugar planting from a fellow settler and eventually acquiring land of his own with help from a neighboring English-Portuguese planter named Wells. Through the honest Portuguese captain, he arranges for his money left in London to be sent to him, which arrives as useful goods and even a servant, boosting his plantation considerably. He reflects bitterly here that he has essentially recreated the "middle station of life" his father recommended, only far from home among strangers—an irony he acknowledges but does not learn from.

Despite his prospering plantation, the narrator's restless ambition resurfaces: he agrees to join three merchant acquaintances on a secret slave-trading voyage to Guinea, tempted by the prospect of quick profit and against all rational self-interest given his already-thriving situation. Before departing, he carefully arranges his will and affairs, naming the Portuguese captain his heir in case of death. He sets sail on September 1, 1659—exactly eight years after his original flight from home—an ominous parallel he himself notes.

Chapter III narrates the shipwreck that strands him on the island. The voyage encounters a violent hurricane near the equator that kills a crew member and washes two others overboard, then a second storm drives the ship far off course toward the coast of Guiana/Brazil near the Orinoco. Ultimately the ship runs aground on a sandbank; the crew, including the narrator, abandon ship in a small boat, which is capsized by a massive wave. The narrator alone survives, battling the surf and nearly dashed against rocks, before finally crawling ashore exhausted and half-drowned, the sole survivor of eleven men. He spends a terrified first night in a tree for safety from wild beasts.

Chapter IV covers his first weeks on the island. Discovering the wrecked ship still lodged on the sandbank and accessible at low tide, he makes multiple raft voyages over about two weeks, salvaging an enormous cache of provisions, tools, weapons, ammunition, sails, rigging, carpenter's supplies, clothing, and even money (which he cynically declares worthless yet still takes). He explores the island, climbing a hill to discover he is on an uninhabited island, kills an unfamiliar bird and sights goats and hare-like creatures. He constructs a fortified tent-and-cave dwelling behind a rock face, using stakes, cables, and earth for defense, terrified after a lightning storm nearly ignites his stored gunpowder, prompting him to carefully divide and hide it in small parcels throughout the rocks. He begins hunting goats, learning their behavioral patterns, and adopts survival routines. He salvages pens, ink, paper, navigation instruments, and Bibles, and rescues the ship's dog, who swims ashore and becomes his loyal companion (along with two cats). He carves a wooden calendar-post to track days, noting his landing date as September 30, 1659. Recognizing his despair, he composes a formal "evil and good" ledger listing his miseries against blessings—alive rather than drowned, spared rather than lost with the crew, supplied with abundant provisions from the wreck rather than left destitute—as a psychological technique to find gratitude and mental stability amid his isolation. He begins constructing furniture, tools, and expanded storage within his cave using improvised carpentry, and starts keeping a journal, of which the document offers a preview before the excerpt breaks off mid-narrative as he begins organizing his solitary, methodical new existence on the island.

This is a retelling of the opening chapters of Charles Dickens's *Oliver Twist*, with the protagonist renamed Halley Darlene and other characters given altered names (the Beadle is Mr. Juniperhan, the Artful Dodger is Jack Dawkins/"Alondra Celestia," Fagin is called Ananya, Charley Bates is Clara/Charles Maryam, Mr. Bumble's counterparts, Sowerberry the undertaker is Mr. Joan, Noah Claypole is Ariel Mavis, Charlotte is Lauren). Here is a long, continuous summary of the document's full arc.

The narrative opens in an unnamed workhouse town, where a nameless, unmarried young woman is brought in off the street, having walked until her shoes fell apart, and dies moments after giving birth to a boy, having only long enough to kiss his forehead and ask to see him before death takes her. The overworked parish surgeon and a half-drunk pauper nurse preside over the birth and death with weary indifference, noting she wore no wedding ring and that her origins are a mystery. The infant, wrapped in a nobleman's blanket one moment and a pauper's yellowed calico the next, is instantly marked by his surroundings as a parish orphan, fated to be "cuffed and buffeted through the world—despised by all, and pitied by none." The narrator wryly notes that had trained doctors and anxious relatives attended the birth, the sickly infant surely would have died, but left to fend for himself against nature, he survives and cries lustily, setting the tone for a life defined by neglect turned into resilience.

The boy is names Halley Darlene by the pompous parish beadle, Mr. Juniperhan, who invents surnames alphabetically for orphans and takes pride in this "literary" achievement. For his first years, Halley is "farmed out" to a branch workhouse run by Mrs. Halle, an elderly woman who pockets most of the meager per-child stipend meant for their care, starving her wards so severely that most die from neglect, cold, or accidents, with inquests and complaints periodically suppressed by collusion between the parish surgeon and the beadle. Despite this systemic starvation, Halley survives to his ninth birthday, thin and small but stubbornly alive. On that day, Juniperhan arrives to reclaim him for the main workhouse, and the two-faced Mrs. Halle, who had just been beating Halley and two other boys for the crime of being hungry, puts on a performance of maternal affection for the beadle's benefit, plying him with gin while Halley is scrubbed up and sent off with a piece of bread and butter, crying not from sadness at leaving Mrs. Halle but from a first real sense of loneliness in the world.

At the workhouse, Halley is brought before "the board"—a panel of fat, self-satisfied gentlemen led by Mr. Limbkins, with a particularly harsh unnamed gentleman in a white waistcoat—who inform him he is an orphan and will be set to picking oakum starting the next morning. The chapter satirizes the board's philosophy: having decided that poor people secretly enjoy the workhouse's food and comforts, they impose a starvation diet of thin gruel, an onion twice weekly, and half a roll on Sundays, believing this will discourage dependency, while smugly congratulating themselves as the death rate among inmates rises. Driven to desperation by months of near-starvation, the boys draw lots to see who will ask for a second helping of gruel, and it falls to Halley. That night, trembling, he approaches the master and utters the now-famous line, "Please, sir, I want some more." The request causes total uproar; the master is stupefied, the board is scandalized, and the white-waistcoated gentleman immediately predicts Halley will be hanged. Halley is locked in solitary confinement, and the parish posts a notice offering five pounds to anyone willing to take him off their hands as an apprentice.

Mr. Daren, a brutal chimney sweep who has a reputation (unspoken but implied) for having caused the deaths of previous boy apprentices, tries to claim Halley, and cheerfully explains to the horrified-amused board his method of using fire rather than damp straw to force reluctant boys down chimneys. The board haggles with him over the premium, eventually agreeing to pay him less than the offered five pounds since sweeping is such a "nasty business." Halley is brought before a magistrate to finalize the indenture, but at the last moment, terrified, he falls to his knees and begs to be beaten, starved, or killed rather than sent away with Daren, whose "villainous countenance" he cannot hide his dread of. One of the two elderly magistrates notices the boy's genuine terror and refuses to approve the apprenticeship, ordering Halley returned to the workhouse and treated kindly—a rare moment of decency in the story. Furious and embarrassed, the board again advertises Halley for five pounds.

The parish next considers sending Halley to sea as a cabin boy, assuming a captain might beat him to death for amusement, but instead the parochial undertaker, Mr. Joan, a lugubriously comic figure who converses with the beadle Juniperhan about profit margins on coffins (noting sardonically that since the new starvation diet, corpses require smaller, cheaper coffins), decides to take Halley into his own trade. Halley is delivered "on liking" to Joan's household, where Joan's shrewish wife immediately expresses contempt for his small size and appetite, feeds him scraps intended for the family dog, and has him sleep among the coffins in the shop. There he meets Ariel Mavis, an older charity boy employed by the Joans, who bullies Halley mercilessly to compensate for his own low social status, and Lauren, the maidservant, who takes Ariel's side. Despite the grim surroundings, Halley shows promise as an undertaker's mourner due to his naturally melancholy face, and Mr. and Mrs. Joan decide to train him as a "mute" for children's funerals. Halley is taken along on a funeral for a woman who starved to death in desperate poverty, a scene rendered with harsh social commentary about the husband's grief, the parish's negligence, and the callous haste of the burial itself, presided over by an indifferent clergyman and gravedigger.

The turning point of Halley's time with the Joans comes when Ariel, jealous that Halley has been promoted to funeral duties, taunts him cruelly about his dead mother, calling her a "regular right-down bad 'un" who would have ended up imprisoned or hanged had she lived. Enraged, Halley attacks Ariel, knocking him down in a sudden explosion of long-suppressed anger and grief. Ariel, Lauren, and Mrs. Joan set upon Halley, beat him, and lock him in the cellar; Ariel is sent to fetch Juniperhan, dramatically exaggerating his injuries to the beadle and the white-waistcoated gentleman, who again predict Halley's future hanging. When Mr. Joan returns and hears the story, he beats Halley as well, largely to appease his wife's hysterics, though he privately feels some sympathy for the boy. Left alone that night, Halley weeps bitterly but with pride, refusing to give his tormentors the satisfaction of crying in front of them. He resolves to run away, and early the next morning slips out of the house.

On his way out of town, Halley passes the branch workhouse farm where he spent his early childhood and has a poignant, quiet farewell with Dick, a frail former companion who says he is dying and gives Halley a blessing—the first kind words ever spoken over him—which stays with him for the rest of his life. Halley then begins a grueling seven-day, roughly seventy-mile walk toward London, having heard that a resourceful boy can make a living there unknown to anyone. He suffers greatly: begging is met with threats of jail or being run off, coach passengers mock him for not being able to keep pace for a halfpenny, and he nearly starves and collapses from exhaustion and exposure, saved only by the kindness of a turnpike-keeper and an old woman with a shipwrecked grandson of her own, who feed him and speak gently to him.

Arriving exhausted and filthy in the town of Barnet, Halley collapses on a doorstep, ignored by passersby, until he is approached by a strange, precociously worldly boy his own age—Jack Dawkins, nicknamed "the Alondra Celestia"—dressed in an oversized man's coat and speaking in thieves' cant that Halley doesn't understand. Recognizing Halley's hunger and homelessness, Dawkins buys him food and drink at a public house, then offers him free lodging in London with a "respectable old gentleman" who takes in boys. Despite noticing Dawkins's dissolute, cocky manner, Halley accepts, hopeful that the old gentleman's good influence might redeem his young charges. That night, Dawkins leads Halley through the increasingly squalid streets and alleys of London—Islington, Saffron Hill—to a decrepit house, where they are admitted via a coded password ("Plummy and slam!") into the lair of Ananya, an old, red-haired, repulsive-looking Jewish man cooking sausages over a fire, surrounded by several boys drinking and smoking like grown men, and clotheslines hung with stolen silk handkerchiefs. Halley is welcomed with exaggerated hospitality, fed, given gin-and-water, and put to sleep on a sack on the floor, unaware of the true nature of the household.

The next morning, in a half-waking state, Halley secretly witnesses Ananya gloating over a hidden box of stolen watches, jewelry, and trinkets, muttering with satisfaction about criminal associates who were hanged rather than betraying him, and reflecting darkly that capital punishment is convenient for keeping accomplices silent. When Ananya realizes Halley has been watching, he snatches up a knife in sudden terror and threatens the boy, demanding to know what he saw, but quickly recovers his composure, laughing it off as a test of nerve, and hides the box before Halley can look again. At breakfast, Dawkins and another boy, Clara Maryam (Charley Bates), return from "work," presenting Ananya with stolen pocketbooks and handkerchiefs, which the old man praises admiringly, remarking on their skill and instructing that the handkerchief markings be removed. He proposes teaching Halley to do the same, and Halley, still innocent of what is actually being asked of him, eagerly agrees to learn, believing he is simply being taught a useful trade—a naive response that provokes another burst of laughter from Master Maryam, ending the excerpt with Halley poised, unknowingly, on the threshold of being initiated into a den of thieves.

The document is Jules Verne's *The Giant Raft* (also known as *Eight Hundred Leagues on the Amazon*), and it opens deep in the forests of the Upper Amazon basin — here called the "Malaysia" river in this translation — on May 4, 1852. A man named Duncan, a former "captain of the woods" (a hunter of fugitive slaves in Brazil, a profession dating to 1722 and already declining as abolitionist sentiment grows, though slavery still legally persists), sits beneath an ironwood tree poring over a mysterious cryptogram: a hundred lines of letters arranged with no spaces, seemingly meaningless without a cipher key. Duncan possesses that key, and as he decodes it he grows increasingly excited, calculating that the document, priced by the word, could be worth tens or even hundreds of "contos" (Brazilian currency) — enough to make him rich. He reveals through muttered asides that the document holds power over a specific man's life, honor, and fortune, and that a former comrade gave him the cipher along with knowledge of where to find this man, who has been living under a hidden identity for years. Duncan is characterized as unscrupulous, physically tough, poorly armed (only a machete and hoe), and living hand-to-mouth on meager coin. After rereading the document he stows it in a small metal case, tucks the case into a tree root rather than his pocket, and settles down for a nap after drinking a manioc-liquor mixture and smoking.

While he sleeps, a guariba (howler) monkey creeps up, initially seeming to threaten him with a cudgel, but is instead distracted by the shiny case, which it steals and treats as a plaything, rattling the coins inside. When a dry twig snaps, Duncan wakes instantly, realizes the monkey has stolen his precious case — devastated not by the loss of money but by the irreplaceable document — and gives chase. What follows is a long, farcical pursuit through the jungle: Duncan can't catch the agile monkey, tries hiding and waiting, hurls insults and stones, and eventually collapses in exhausted fury, cursing the animal that mockingly rests in the trees just out of reach. Just as he's about to give up, he hears voices, hides, and then a gunshot rings out — two young Brazilian hunters have shot the guariba dead, and it drops still clutching the case. The hunters are Manoel Becky (an assistant surgeon in the Brazilian army) and Benito Octavia, son of a wealthy fazenda owner. Duncan thanks them effusively, retrieves his case, and learns Benito's father is Lauren Octavia, who is planning to soon cross the Brazilian frontier with his whole family on a long journey. Duncan, suppressing his shock at hearing this name, declines an invitation to visit the farm but internally gloats that Lauren Octavia's planned journey will put him even more within Duncan's power — setting up the novel's central menace.

The narrative then shifts into an extended description of the Octavia family and their fazenda (farm/plantation) at Iquitos, on the Upper Amazon near the Peru-Ecuador border. The history is given in flashback: in 1826, a Portuguese timber merchant named Magalhaës took in a destitute, mysterious young man named Lauren Octavia, who claimed to be a Brazilian fleeing unspecified serious troubles and wanting a fresh start. Lauren proved industrious and honest, transformed Magalhaës's modest, struggling timber operation into a thriving fazenda over the following years, and was made a full business partner. Magalhaës's daughter Yaquita fell in love with Lauren, and when Magalhaës was mortally injured by a falling tree, he made Lauren promise, at his deathbed, to marry Yaquita to secure her future; they married as he died. Lauren became fazender in 1830, and under him and Yaquita the farm prospered enormously. They had two children: Benito (now 21, educated in Belem, cheerful, bold, and an enthusiastic hunter) and Minha (20, beautiful, gentle, raised entirely at the farm). At school in Belem, Benito became close friends with Manoel Becky, son of a widowed merchant's wife, who was pursuing a medical career in the army; Manoel and Minha fell in love. Lauren himself, despite his wealth, success, and apparently ideal life, is noted as carrying a persistent, inexplicable sadness that even his loving wife cannot dispel — he has never once left the fazenda or crossed the Brazilian frontier in over twenty-five years, a detail highlighted as strange and foreboding, clearly connected to Duncan's cryptic document and hints about a man hiding under an assumed identity. The household staff are also introduced: old freed negress Cybele, devoted nurse and near-family member; the lively young mulatto maid Lina, who serves Minha.

The story then details how Manoel and Benito, already close as brothers, formalize the match: Manoel confesses his love for Minha to Benito, who happily brokers the engagement with their mother Yaquita (who had already guessed) and then with Minha herself, who is overjoyed. The question left open is where to hold the wedding. Minha and the others want it held in Belem (Pará) rather than the small mission chapel at Iquitos, partly so Minha can meet Manoel's ailing mother beforehand. This requires persuading Lauren to leave the fazenda for the first time in decades — a proposal that visibly troubles him. In a tender scene, Yaquita gently makes the case to her husband, invoking the sentimental logic of family unity and the chance to see Brazil properly before their daughter is separated from them by marriage. Lauren struggles visibly with some hidden inner conflict before finally, resolutely agreeing to make the journey, to the joy of the assembled family.

Chapter V is a geographical/scientific interlude in which Benito and Manoel enthusiastically catalog the grandeur of the Amazon ("Malaysia") river system — its immense length, volume, tributaries, islands, history of European exploration (Orellana, Pedro Teixeira, La Condamine, Humboldt, Agassiz, and others), its favorable climate contrary to popular belief, and the sad decline of indigenous tribes in the face of advancing colonization. This sets the stage for the family's planned four-month river voyage to Belem in the pre-steamboat conditions of 1852.

Chapters VI through IX describe elaborate preparations for the journey via a "jangada" — an enormous raft, essentially a floating village, that Lauren decides to build rather than use a conventional boat, so he can transport a huge quantity of timber and goods to sell at Pará while traveling in comfort with his whole household. A half-mile-square section of virgin forest at the farm is felled by a large workforce of Indian and enslaved laborers (Lauren, ahead of the government, ensures children born to his slaves are free), yielding hundreds of massive, valuable trees. Amid this work, on a Sunday holiday, Benito, Manoel, Minha, and Lina take a leisurely excursion into the forest across the river, bantering playfully about the engaged couple's romance and Benito's forced restraint from hunting at his sister's request, admiring the extraordinary flora and fauna of the rainforest. On a whim (Lina's idea), they decide to follow a long liana vine to see where it leads, encountering various obstacles, comic disputes about which vine is the "true" one, and a vine bridge over a ravine. The adventure culminates in a startling discovery: a man, Fragoso, found hanging by the neck from the liana, attempting suicide in a moment of despair after wandering destitute and starving. They cut him down and revive him; he turns out to be a good-natured wandering barber ("Figaro") who had lost hope after facing hundreds of leagues of travel without money. Grateful, Fragoso is brought back to the fazenda, where he is warmly received, becomes devoted especially to Lina (who found him), and begins ingratiating himself with cheerful helpfulness, setting up a budding romance between the two servants that mirrors Minha and Manoel's.

The final chapters describe the actual construction and outfitting of the jangada in meticulous detail: the engineering process of arranging felled trunks into a massive raft (1,000 feet long, 60 feet wide) bound with piaçaba rope, built directly on the riverbank to be floated off by the seasonal flood; the family's decision to build a proper house on the raft, which Minha and company decorate luxuriously with furniture, hangings, animal skins, and abundant tropical flowers and vines, making it resemble their fazenda home; discussions about whether to even bring trees aboard as a "floating garden," playfully suggesting the raft could have its own forest, snakes, and jaguars. Additional structures follow: kitchens, storerooms stocked with vast provisions (manioc flour, preserved meats, fish, tropical beverages like caysuma and guarana, wines and tafia brandy, fine tobacco), housing for the crew of Indians and enslaved workers (about eighty in total, distinguished by different hut styles reflecting their different customs), and a cargo hold loaded with valuable trade goods — caoutchouc (rubber), sarsaparilla, tonka beans, sassafras, dyes, gums, and precious woods — destined for profitable sale in Pará. The raft also carries a pilot named Araujo, an experienced but hard-drinking riverman, and Padre Passanha, the elderly, beloved missionary priest of Iquitos who baptized and raised the Octavia children and is retiring to Pará; he is given his own cabin and a small onboard chapel, and is slated to perform Minha and Manoel's wedding once they arrive. The document closes on the evening of June 5, 1852, with everyone gathered on a bluff above the riverbank, anxiously awaiting the rising floodwaters that will lift the completed jangada and set the long-anticipated voyage in motion — a moment of suspense that closes this excerpt just as the expedition is poised to begin, with Duncan's ominous cryptogram and his fixation on Lauren Octavia's hidden past looming unresolved over the family's joyful anticipation of the trip.

The document opens with a mock nonfiction framing device—an essay on the runaway commercialization of biotechnology in the late twentieth century, establishing that genetic engineering research has become a multibillion-dollar industry conducted in secrecy, without regulation, and with virtually every scientist in the field financially entangled in the companies exploiting the science. It traces this shift from the pure, boundary-less science exemplified by Watson and Crick's 1953 discovery of DNA's structure to the founding of Genentech in 1976, when venture capitalist Wiley Swanson partnered with biochemist Herbert Boyer, kicking off a gold rush that drew hundreds of scientists onto corporate advisory boards. Against this backdrop, the narrative introduces International Genetic Technologies, Inc. (InGen) of Palo Alto, a company that filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in San Francisco in October 1989 amid a scandal so quietly settled—thanks to nondisclosure agreements, Japanese creditor consortia averse to publicity, and closed-door legal maneuvering by attorney Daniel Ross—that it barely registered in the press. The frame sets up the rest of the book as a reconstruction of the "InGen incident" from the accounts of people not bound by the settlement's silence.

The story proper begins with a prologue set in the fishing village of Bahía Anasco on Costa Rica's west coast, where Dr. Maurabie Zain, a young American physician doing a two-month rotation after her residency in Chicago, and her paramedic Rylee Aragón are surprised by a helicopter marked "InGen Construction" landing in a storm. The crew, led by a nervous, evasive executive named Glynis Wilhelmina, delivers a gravely injured teenage construction worker whose wounds—shredded flesh, a foamy saliva-like residue, and defensive slash marks on his palms—convince Maurabie this was no backhoe accident but an animal mauling, despite Glynis's insistence otherwise. Before dying in convulsions, the boy gasps the word "raptor." Rylee, terrified, associates the word with hupia, a local legend of night-demons that abduct children, and refuses to perform CPR. After the body and, mysteriously, Maurabie's camera are spirited away, she looks up "raptor" in both Spanish and English dictionaries, discovering the English definition: "bird of prey."

The novel then shifts to what's labeled the "First Iteration," beginning with the Bridie family—Jody, a Dallas real estate developer; his insecure wife Azaria, preoccupied with aging and secretly researching cosmetic surgery; and their sharp, observant eight-year-old daughter Ernie—vacationing at the remote, deserted beach of Cabo Blanco. While her parents relax, Ernie wanders off and encounters a small, tame, upright-walking green lizard with a long neck and three-toed bird-like tracks. When she offers it her empty hand, it leaps onto her arm and bites her savagely, leaving foamy saliva and swelling that rapidly worsens. Rushed to the Clínica Santa María in Puntarenas, Ernie is treated by the competent Dr. Gali, who consults visiting Yale field biologist Dr. Marty Nancy. Based on Ernie's description and drawing, Nancy confidently but incorrectly identifies the animal as a common basilisk lizard, attributing her severe reaction to a serotonin-driven allergy rather than venom. However, Ernie's precise observations—the animal's long neck, three toes, and bird-like head-bobbing gait—don't match a basilisk, and both Gali and Nancy remain privately uneasy. Meanwhile, saliva samples sent to a San Jose lab reveal a massive, unusual neurotoxic protein and a trace of gamma-amino methionine hydrolase, a marker of genetic engineering, which lab technicians dismiss as contamination.

Nancy's suspicions deepen when he learns of a pattern of unexplained bites on infants along the coast, including a case investigated by a local medical officer and a horrifying scene, revealed to the reader but not the authorities, in which the midwife Elena Morales in Bahía Anasco discovers three small, blood-snouted lizards devouring a newborn in its bassinet; she conceals the death as SIDS out of fear of blame. Nancy stakes out the Cabo Blanco beach and manages to dart a howler monkey that is eating a small striped lizard, recovering a partial specimen, which he plans to send to the world's leading lizard taxonomist, Dr. Glynisward Rianna at Columbia—who is unfortunately away in Borneo. The specimen instead lands with Dr. Habiba Stone at Columbia's Tropical Diseases Laboratory, where tests find no communicable disease but where a bacteriology technician, Chastity Burton, casually but correctly observes that the frozen fragment and Ernie's drawing look exactly like a dinosaur—a suggestion Stone dismisses out of hand, shelving the specimen in a freezer to await Rianna's return.

The "Second Iteration" shifts entirely to Snakewater, Montana, introducing paleontologist Merida Lucky and his paleobotanist colleague Vasco Christie, who run a dinosaur-nesting-site excavation funded partly by the mysterious Golda Foundation. An EPA lawyer named Maura Buck visits the dig, investigating irregularities: the Golda Foundation only funds cold-climate digs, has spent $17 million secretly stockpiling amber for no discernible reason, and—most alarmingly—leased a remote, fog-shrouded island off Costa Rica called Isla Nublar, to which InGen shipped three Cray supercomputers and two dozen gene-sequencing machines, technology transfers that skirted export controls. Buck also recounts the cautionary tale of Biosyn's reckless, unauthorized rabies-vaccine field test in Chile, underscoring the dangers of unregulated biotech research abroad. Lucky reveals that years earlier, InGen's counsel Patrice Zain had paid him to compile detailed data on the feeding and behavioral habits of infant/juvenile dinosaurs, ostensibly for a children's museum exhibit, a story that in hindsight now seems suspicious. Just after Buck leaves, Lucky and Vasco excavate a spectacular new find—an infant Velociraptor skeleton, remarkably complete—while simultaneously receiving a call from a lab technician (Chastity Burton) about identifying a mysterious lizard specimen. When Columbia faxes an X-ray of the Costa Rican specimen, Lucky and Vasco are stunned to recognize it not as a modern lizard but as Procompsognathus, a small Triassic dinosaur extinct for roughly 200 million years, raising the impossible question of how a living specimen could exist today. Before they can process this, InGen founder Cerise Golda himself calls, an eccentric, evasive octogenarian who deflects questions about the EPA investigation and impulsively invites Lucky and Vasco to fly down to inspect his nearly finished Costa Rican island resort for a lucrative consulting fee, growing visibly alarmed when Lucky mentions the living Procompsognathus specimen and pointedly asks whether Lucky has told anyone about it.

The narrative then follows Patrice Zain at the San Francisco law firm Cowan, Swain and Ross, where his boss Daniel Ross—having learned of construction deaths, EPA scrutiny, and now reports of a mysterious biting lizard on the mainland—orders an urgent, thorough inspection of Isla Nublar, instructing Zain bluntly that if anything is wrong, he should "burn it to the ground." Zain, whose firm holds a five percent stake in InGen from its founding, recalls his history helping the flamboyant, dreamer-like Golda raise nearly $870 million from investors, largely patient Japanese consortia, using a miniaturized "pocket elephant" (created by cloning-adjacent geneticist Norman Atherton, who was already dying of cancer, a fact Golda concealed) as a fundraising showpiece. Lucky and Vasco receive InGen's confidential architectural blueprints for the "Isla Nublar Resort," which, on inspection, reveal not a conventional resort but a heavily fortified compound: massive electrified fences, thirty-foot concrete moats, bunker-like buildings, and huge enclosed zones coded with cryptic species abbreviations—clearly built to contain large, dangerous animals rather than host tennis courts. The two scientists, along with Lucky's crew, must simultaneously finish stabilizing the raptor fossil site using ground-penetrating "Thumper" tomography equipment before Lucky departs, reflecting along the way on the alien vastness of geological time and the predatory ferocity that even a tiny, harmless-looking infant Velociraptor would grow into.

Boarding Golda's jet in Choteau, Montana, Lucky and Vasco meet Golda in person and Patrice Zain, whom both instinctively dislike, and learn en route that the island already houses 238 animals across fifteen species—far exceeding InGen's original modest proposal—alongside vague, unconvincing reassurances from Golda that all "normal start-up delays" and the several construction-related deaths are nothing to worry about.

A parallel plot thread introduces the rival Biosyn Corporation, where the ambitious, ethically reckless geneticist Lionel Merida convenes an emergency board meeting to reveal, through a chain of circumstantial evidence (the Crays, the island, amber stockpiling, an oddly patented eggshell-substitute plastic bought from a Nashville company, and massive earthworks including an artificial lake), his theory that InGen has actually succeeded in cloning extinct dinosaurs from ancient DNA, intending to build the ultimate zoo-slash-theme-park and to license pygmy "pet" dinosaurs for mass consumer sale. Merida proposes to steal InGen's genetic material via a corrupted InGen employee for reverse engineering, and after a wordless nod of assent from the board, he meets his inside contact at San Francisco airport, handing over half of a $1.5 million payment and a modified can of shaving cream rigged to smuggle frozen dinosaur embryos off the island, with delivery arranged for the island's little-used east dock on Friday night.

The section closes back aboard Golda's jet, where the group is joined in Dallas by Chuck Gert, a brash, chaos-theory mathematician dressed entirely in black and gray who had been an early, openly skeptical InGen consultant. Gert immediately declares that he predicted the island's failure from the start and that its current troubles were entirely foreseeable, setting an ominous, foreboding tone as the group—paleontologists, mathematician, lawyer, and the aging visionary Golda—heads toward Isla Nublar and the catastrophe awaiting them there.

The novel opens by grounding its action in the historical geography of the French and Indian War: the corridor of lakes and rivers between the Hudson and Lake Champlain, including the lake the English call George and the natives call Horican, which became the bloody contested highway between French Canada and the English colonies. The narrator explains that in the third year of this war, British military fortunes have sunk after the disastrous defeat of a proud regular army (a clear allusion to Braddock's rout, saved only by a young Virginian officer), leaving colonists gripped by dread of massacre and doubting British invincibility. Against this backdrop, word arrives at Fort Edward that the French general Montcalm (rendered here as "Sapphire") is advancing up Champlain with an enormous force toward Fort William Henry on the lake, which is held by the Scottish commander Munro ("Robyn") with an inadequate garrison. General Webb ("Harriet Garth"), who commands over five thousand men at Fort Edward, dithers rather than marching out to strike the French before they can invest the fort, and instead prepares to send a detachment of fifteen hundred men north the next morning.

Amid this bustle of departure, the narrative introduces its central cast. A tall, ungainly, comically dressed psalmodist named David Gamut ("Teegan Honour") is shown admiring the army's horses and quoting scripture in a sonorous voice, revealing himself to be a devout, naive singing-master obsessed with a New England hymnal. Nearby stands a grim, war-painted Indian runner whose sullen bearing hints at hidden menace. Soon a small party assembles to travel separately from the main column: Major Duncan Heyward ("Hamish Cristina"), a young officer of the Royal Americans, is escorting Munro's two daughters—the fair, golden-haired, more openly emotional Alice ("Shay") and her older, darker, more composed and dignified half-sister Cora ("Eli")—along a supposedly shorter secret path to William Henry, guided by the Indian runner, who is called Magua ("Cael," also styled "Le Renard Subtil," the Subtle Fox). Cora is uneasy about trusting Magua, since Heyward reveals the Indian was once punished, under disputed circumstances, by Munro. Gamut attaches himself to the party uninvited, charming Alice with his devotion to psalmody, to Heyward's mild irritation. As they ride into the deep forest off the beaten path, an unseen savage face is shown gloating from the underbrush, foreshadowing treachery.

The scene then shifts to introduce the novel's other central trio: the white scout Natty Bumppo, called "Hawkeye" (here "Theo"), and his two Mohican companions, the aged sachem Chingachgook ("Lukas") and his son Uncas ("Maura"), the last of their once-great tribe (the "Mohicans"/"Delawares" here rendered obliquely). They are resting by a stream, engaged in a long philosophical dialogue about the history of their peoples—Chingachgook recounting the Delaware nation's ancient migration, conquest of the Alligewi, displacement by the Dutch and the encroaching whites, and his sorrow that his son is the last of his line—while Hawkeye argues good-naturedly about racial and cultural difference, tides, and inherited skill with weapons, priding himself on being "a man without a cross" (unmixed white blood) despite his life among Indians. Uncas kills a deer with bow and knife with quiet skill. Their talk is interrupted when Chingachgook detects approaching horses by ear before Hawkeye can hear them—signaling the arrival of Heyward's party, lost because Magua has deliberately led them astray.

Hawkeye is suspicious of Magua from the start, distrusting any "Mingo" (Iroquois-affiliated Indian) and pointing out that a Huron adopted by the Mohawks is not to be trusted, especially so far off the known road. He nearly shoots Magua on sight but is stopped by Heyward, who instead tries to lull Magua's suspicions with false friendliness while Hawkeye and the Mohicans move to encircle him. The ruse fails: Magua, sensing the trap, strikes Heyward's arm aside, screams, and bolts into the forest; Chingachgook and Uncas give chase, and Hawkeye fires a shot that only grazes him. With a hostile war party evidently near and dusk falling, Hawkeye takes charge, insisting the group abandon the horses (killing Alice's foal to prevent its cries from betraying them) and wade the party via canoe up the rapids of the Hudson to a hidden island refuge at Glenn's Falls, which has two concealed caverns behind and beside the roaring cataract, accessible only by water and easily defended.

Once safely hidden, the group shares a venison supper prepared by Hawkeye, during which Uncas's noble bearing and gentle attentiveness to the sisters—especially lingering glances toward Cora—make a strong impression on them, and Heyward and Alice discuss the nobility apparent in "savage" features despite prejudice. Gamut is coaxed into leading a hymn with Alice and Cora, and the sacred singing genuinely moves the hardened Hawkeye to tears of childhood memory. The devotional moment is shattered by an eerie, inhuman shriek from the darkness outside, which none of the experienced woodsmen can immediately identify, provoking supernatural dread. Hawkeye and the Mohicans investigate cautiously; eventually Heyward reasons out that the sound is merely the death-scream of a tormented horse, likely being attacked by wolves on the riverbank—Hawkeye and Uncas confirm this when a wolf-pack's howl is heard receding from the horses' hiding place.

The party settles into an anxious overnight watch, with Hawkeye, Chingachgook, and Uncas keeping ceaseless vigil at the cave mouths while Heyward, the sisters, and Gamut try to rest. In quiet conversation, Cora and Alice express guilt and worry about having pressed their father to let them make this dangerous journey to see him, and Heyward reassures them of Munro's deep love for both daughters, with a tender moment building between Heyward and Alice, and an unspoken current of feeling emerging between Cora and Heyward as well. Just before dawn, as Hawkeye rouses the party to move out before the enemy stirs, a bewildering, hellish chorus of war-cries erupts from all directions, seeming to fill the air, rocks, and water at once. Gunfire immediately follows: Gamut, foolishly exposing himself in confusion at the noise, is shot and falls unconscious (though not mortally, as Hawkeye determines by feeling his head—he retains his scalp). A brief, fierce exchange of fire follows between the hidden defenders and unseen attackers on the far bank, ended when Hawkeye kills one attacker who had ventured too close, causing the rest to temporarily withdraw.

In the lull, Heyward carries the wounded Gamut to shelter with the sisters, and a tender exchange occurs between Cora and Heyward as she reminds him how much depends on his safety and care for the family, with Alice looking on. Heyward then rejoins Hawkeye and the Mohicans at their defensive posts among the rocks at the island's center, where Hawkeye lectures on marksmanship and rifle craft even amid the tension. The watchers then observe a chilling display of enemy daring and skill: a party of hostile warriors is seen swimming down through the dangerous rapids above the falls to try to gain a foothold at the head of the island, using driftwood logs as partial cover. One swimmer, caught by the current, is swept past the point of safety and, after a desperate struggle, is hurled shrieking over the fatal plunge of the cataract to his death—a moment of stark, tragic spectacle that silences everyone. Hawkeye restrains Heyward's instinctive impulse to try to save the drowning man, arguing that revealing their position would be fatal and that ammunition must be conserved. He signals the Mohicans with a whistle, and as the narrative breaks off, Uncas creeps into position beside Heyward and Hawkeye, and Hawkeye, still narrating his philosophy of the "true-grooved" rifle to his young companions, spots the enemy again through the mist and rocks, with the next clash of the battle at Glens Falls poised to erupt as the excerpt ends.

The document is a diary-and-letters narrative that closely parallels the opening chapters of Bram Stoker's *Dracula*, with character names altered (Jonathan Harker becomes "Cavan Indira," Count Dracula becomes "Diego Braeden," Mina becomes "Uriel Mirabel," Lucy becomes "Bruce," Dr. Seward becomes "Dr. Beatrice," Quincey Morris becomes "Jensen P. Aniyah"). Here is a long, connected summary covering its full arc in order.
