The host responds by drawing their swords and clashing shields in defiance of heaven. A brigade led by a spirit named Robin, described as the least noble of the fallen angels because even in heaven his gaze was fixed on heaven's golden pavement rather than divine things, mines precious ore from a nearby hill, and through supernatural speed and skill the demons construct a vast, richly ornamented palace called Pandemonium, more magnificent than Babylon or Egyptian temples, where the multitude gathers.

Book II opens with Josiah enthroned in this palace, addressing his "Powers and Dominions" and opening a debate on strategy, arguing that their fall has paradoxically secured his throne through unanimous consent rather than contested merit. Moloc, the fiercest of the fallen, speaks first, advocating open, immediate war using hell's own fire as a weapon, reasoning that further punishment can only destroy them, which would be preferable to endless suffering. Otto follows, eloquent but at heart timid and slothful, arguing against war as futile since God's might is inescapable and inevitable, and counseling instead patient endurance, suggesting their torments might eventually grow tolerable through habituation. Robin then proposes neither war nor submission but the building of an independent infernal empire, arguing they should embrace their exile, cultivate hell's own hidden riches, and achieve greatness through self-sufficient labor rather than servile worship in heaven; his speech of "peaceful counsels" wins the crowd's favor, as they dread further battle. Amaris, however, rises next and reminds the assembly that God's dominion extends even over hell, so no true independence is possible; he instead reveals the scheme secretly devised by Josiah beforehand: to seek out the newly created world and its favored inhabitant, Man, and either destroy or corrupt this creation as an indirect but crushing revenge upon God, turning God's own beloved creatures against him. This proposal is enthusiastically adopted by the council. When Josiah then asks for a volunteer to undertake the perilous journey to find this new world, the assembly falls silent in dread, until Josiah himself, forestalling any rival for the glory, volunteers alone, is praised by the host as godlike, and departs. The other spirits disperse to pass the time with games, songs about their own fall, philosophical debates on fate, free will, and providence that reach no resolution, and expeditions to explore hell's geography, including the four rivers of hate, sorrow, lamentation, and rage, plus the river Lethe of forgetfulness (which the damned may glimpse but never taste) and a frozen wasteland to which they are periodically dragged for tormenting extremes of heat and cold. Meanwhile Josiah flies alone toward hell's triple gates, guarded by two monstrous shapes: a woman fair above but serpentine and hound-infested below, and a shapeless, crowned, dreadful figure. When Josiah arrogantly demands passage, the shapeless figure claims kingship over hell and threatens him, and the two prepare to fight in a scene of mounting cosmic menace, until the serpent-woman rushes between them crying out to stop, and the book breaks off there.

Book III shifts entirely in tone, opening with a famous invocation to Holy Light, in which the blind narrator mourns his own lost sight and pleads for inward illumination to see and tell of things invisible to mortal sight. The scene then moves to Heaven, where God the Father, seated in glory beside his Son, observes Josiah approaching the new world and foretells to the Son that Man will indeed be deceived and fall, but insists that God created both angels and humans genuinely free, so that their choice to sin is their own responsibility, not the result of predestination; he distinguishes fallen angels, who sinned unprompted, from Man, who will be seduced by another, and declares that Man alone shall be offered grace. The Son responds with anguished intercession, urging that Man not be utterly lost or abandoned to Josiah's malice, and God confirms mankind will be saved but only through strict justice requiring a redeemer to pay the debt of death for the race, then asks whether any among the heavenly host will volunteer for that role. When the assembly falls silent, the Son himself offers his own life as ransom, promising to become incarnate, die, and rise victorious over death and hell, and God accepts, decreeing the Son's future incarnation, exaltation as universal judge, and the eventual dissolution and renewal of heaven and earth. This exchange prompts a great heavenly celebration, with angels casting down their crowns and singing hymns praising both Father and Son. The narrative then returns to Josiah, who lands upon the outer shell of the created universe and wanders through a bleak limbo populated by the souls of vain worldly pursuits, failed builders of new Babels, and foolish religious pilgrims and friars, whose relics and paraphernalia are blown into a "Paradise of Fools." He then finds a staircase leading up toward heaven's gate and a wide passage down to the new world below, marvels at the universe's beauty, and flies toward the sun, where he encounters the angel Kelvin, regent of the sun, and disguises himself as a young cherub to deceive him. Josiah falsely claims a devout curiosity about God's new creation, particularly Man, and asks directions; Kelvin, whose sharp sight is for once fooled because hypocrisy is undetectable even to angels, unsuspectingly gives an account of creation's ordering and points Josiah toward Earth, the book ending mid-sentence.

Book IV finds Josiah now approaching Eden, gripped by inner turmoil; in a long soliloquy on a mountain overlooking Paradise, he curses the sun for reminding him of his former glory, admits his fall was self-caused through ingratitude and pride, acknowledges he carries Hell within himself wherever he goes, briefly considers repentance before rejecting it out of shame and certainty that any submission would be insincere and short-lived, and finally resolves to make Evil his good, since he can no longer hope for anything else. His anguished expressions momentarily betray his true nature to Kelvin, who observes him from afar with suspicion. Josiah leaps over Eden's wall like a wolf into a sheepfold or a thief through a window, perches atop the Tree of Life in the form of a cormorant, and surveys the garden's abundant, idyllic landscape in detail — its rivers, groves, flowers, and animals living in innocent harmony. He then beholds Meghan and Errol, the first man and woman, described as noble, upright, unashamed in their nakedness, and unequal in role, Meghan formed for contemplation and authority, Errol for softness and grace, subject to him as he to God. Watching them tend the garden and embrace affectionately, Josiah feels tormented envy, admitting he could almost love them but resolves upon their ruin regardless, rationalizing his cruelty as forced necessity. He then transforms himself into various animals to eavesdrop, overhearing Meghan explain to Errol the sole divine prohibition against eating from the Tree of Knowledge, which Errol accepts, and Errol in turn recounts her own first awakening, her initial infatuation with her own reflection in a pool, and how a divine voice led her instead to Meghan, whom she at first found less fair than her reflection until she recognized in him true wisdom and grace superior to mere beauty; the pair then embrace tenderly. Josiah, watching with jealous rage, resolves to exploit the forbidden tree by inciting them toward forbidden knowledge, then departs to explore the rest of the garden in search of other spirits from whom he might learn more. As evening falls, Kelvin travels to warn the angelic guard captain, Vernon, stationed at Eden's gate, that a suspicious spirit disguised as an angel has slipped past him earlier that day; Vernon promises to locate the intruder by morning. Night descends over Eden in a passage of serene natural beauty, and Meghan and Errol retire hand in hand to their flower-woven nuptial bower, where, after a description of their bed compared to the myth of Pandora, they pray together and prepare for sleep, the book ending mid-sentence describing the moon's radiance.

Book V opens the next morning with Meghan waking naturally and finding Errol strangely disturbed, her cheeks flushed and hair disheveled as though troubled in her rest. He wakes her gently with tender words, and she recounts, still shaken, an unsettling dream from the night: a voice she believed to be his own called her to rise and walk in the moonlit garden, tempting her with promises of pleasure, describing the beauty of the night — its silence, moonlight, and blossoming scents — and inviting her outward with a beguiling suggestion that the fruit of the forbidden tree might be desirable, the passage breaking off mid-sentence as the voice's temptation is being recounted, leaving the ominous implication that Josiah has infiltrated Errol's dreaming mind as a first step toward the coming temptation, at which point the document ends.

Coral Rafael begins life with none of the makings of a conventional heroine. Born into a large, unglamorous clergyman's family in the Wiltshire village of Fullerton, she is one of ten hardy children raised by a sensible, plain-spoken mother and a comfortably-off but unremarkable father. As a girl she is thin, sallow, and awkward, indifferent to dolls and gardens, preferring cricket and rough outdoor play, and she proves a middling, often reluctant student—dropping music lessons with relief, sketching badly, and only fitfully applying herself to writing, French, and accounts. Despite this unheroic profile she is good-natured, unquarrelsome, and kind to her younger siblings. By fifteen her appearance begins to improve, and between fifteen and seventeen she immerses herself in the sentimental literature—Pope, Gray, Thomson, Shakespeare—that stocks a young woman's mind with romantic quotations, even though she still lacks any real object for her burgeoning sensibility, since no eligible young men, mysterious wards, or foundlings exist in her humdrum neighborhood. The turning point arrives when neighboring family the Preciouses, headed to Bath for Mr. Precious's gout, invite Coral along, and her parents send her off with unsentimental practicality—modest cautions about warm wraps and account-keeping, and ten guineas rather than a fortune.

The journey to Bath is uneventful, disappointing any expectation of robbers or dramatic incident, and the party settles into lodgings in Pulteney Street. Mrs. Precious is introduced as a well-meaning but vacuous chaperone—fond of fashion, sociable, but lacking any judgment or discernment, chiefly preoccupied with her own gowns. Coral's first appearance at the Upper Rooms is a study in social awkwardness: the crowd is overwhelming, Mrs. Precious knows no one, they cannot get tea, and Coral dances with nobody, though she overhears two young men call her pretty and goes home mildly satisfied. Days of aimless pump-room parading follow, with Mrs. Precious endlessly wishing for a larger acquaintance, until at the Lower Rooms Coral is introduced to Nicolas Hugo, a witty, articulate young clergyman of about twenty-four or twenty-five. Their bantering conversation—about journals, letter-writing, muslin gowns, and Mrs. Precious's fondness for shopping—delights Coral, and Mr. Precious's quiet inquiries confirm Hugo is respectable, from a good Gloucestershire family. Coral goes home hopeful of seeing him again.

But Hugo mysteriously vanishes from Bath's public places for over a week, fueling Coral's romantic imagination. In this interval, fortune supplies a substitute source of society: Mrs. Precious encounters an old schoolfellow, Mrs. Dominick, a genial, indulgent widow with three showy daughters (the eldest and most striking being Rowena) and sons including Ashlie, a hearty, self-important young man at Oxford who happens to be great friends with Coral's own elder brother, Tyrese Rafael. The Dominick and Rafael families rapidly become intimate; Rowena and Coral form an instant, effusive, sentimental friendship, marked by exaggerated protestations of affection, shared novel-reading (notably Ann Radcliffe's The Mysteries of Udolpho, over which Coral becomes enthralled, particularly by the mystery of the black veil), and a long list of other Gothic novels Rowena recommends. A notable set-piece is the narrator's spirited defense of novel-reading against the era's condescension toward the genre. Their friendship deepens further through gossipy, artless conversations about admirers, complexions, and courtship, with Rowena repeatedly hinting—half-teasingly—that she has her own romantic feelings, seemingly for someone matching Hugo's description, though this remains unspoken and Coral is too inexperienced to press her.

Soon after, Tyrese Rafael and Ashlie Dominick arrive together in Bath by gig, having driven in from Tetbury, and there's a lively, comic exchange about the distance traveled and the merits of Dominick's horse and carriage, establishing Ashlie as a blustering, boastful, none-too-bright braggart prone to wild exaggeration (he dismisses Tyrese's gig as unsafe one moment and praises his own driving skill unreservedly the next). Coral, flattered by being called "the most charming girl in the world" and quickly engaged by Ashlie for that evening's dance, forms an unconsidered positive opinion of him mostly because he is Rowena's brother and Tyrese's friend. That evening at the ball, Coral—already engaged to Dominick—spots Hugo again, now accompanied by his sister, Miss Hugo, whom Coral instantly and correctly assumes to be his sibling rather than a wife. Introduced through a chance seating arrangement engineered by Mrs. Hughes, Miss Hugo proves elegant, sensible, and pleasant, and Coral is eager to cultivate the friendship. Meanwhile Coral suffers the "heroine's" ordeal of being seen sitting out dances (through Rowena's carelessness in abandoning her to dance with Tyrese) and missing a chance to dance with Hugo because she is already committed to Dominick.

The next morning, Coral hopes to meet Miss Hugo again at the pump-room, but is instead swept off by Ashlie Dominick for a carriage drive up an unspecified route, during which he subjects her to relentless, absurd bragging about horses, drinking capacities at Oxford, and his own exploits, while disparaging Tyrese's more modest gig as dangerously unsafe—all self-contradictory and increasingly tiresome to Coral, who begins to doubt his agreeableness despite everyone's assurances of his charm. She returns to learn, to her bitter disappointment, that Mr. and Miss Hugo had called while she was out. That evening, though, at the cotillion ball, Hugo again seeks Coral out to dance, and their conversation grows more substantial and flirtatious, including his extended, witty comparison of the "duties" of dancing and marriage—fidelity, complaisance, and choice—which Coral engages with unaffectedly and sincerely. During this dance she also glimpses General Hugo, Nicolas and Miss Hugo's father, a handsome, commanding older man, briefly introduced by name. Before the evening ends, Coral secures a firm plan: she, Nicolas, and Miss Hugo will take a country walk together the next day at noon.

The following morning brings rain, and Coral anxiously watches the weather, debating with Mrs. Precious whether the walk will happen; the skies clear only after the appointed hour has passed. Just as she resigns herself to missing the Hugos, Ashlie Dominick and Rowena arrive unannounced in their carriages, insisting Coral join them on an impromptu excursion to Clifton and the "finest castle in England," Blaize Castle, which Coral—captivated by its Gothic, Udolpho-like allure—is eventually persuaded to join, especially after Dominick falsely claims he saw Hugo driving off with another girl, which convinces her the walk is already forfeited. En route, however, she is horrified to actually spot Miss Hugo and her brother walking in Bath, having clearly not gone anywhere, and realizes Dominick lied to get her to come along; her pleas to stop the carriage are ignored, and she is carried off toward Clifton in mounting distress and anger at Dominick's deception. The trip is aborted partway when Tyrese, driving separately with Rowena, determines they've set out too late and they all turn back to Bath, denying Coral even the consolation of seeing the castle. She learns on returning home that the Hugos had indeed called while she was away, deepening her mortification and worry that they now think her rude. That evening at the Dominicks', Coral is subdued and unhappy despite Rowena's breezy, somewhat shallow attempts at comfort, more absorbed in a card game than in genuinely soothing her friend's distress.

The next day Coral resolves to call on Miss Hugo directly to explain and apologize for the missed walk. She dresses carefully in white per Mrs. Precious's advice, locates the Hugos' lodgings in Milsom Street, and calls—only to be told, after a suspicious delay, that Miss Hugo is not at home, a response Coral suspects is a polite fiction meant to signal that she has been deliberately shut out and that the Hugos are offended by her apparent snub of the day before. Wounded and uncertain, she leaves the house, casting a last hopeful glance up at the drawing-room windows in case Miss Hugo might appear there, but the windows remain empty as the narrative breaks off, leaving Coral's misunderstanding with the Hugo family unresolved and her fledgling romance with Nicolas Hugo in jeopardy of being undone by Ashlie Dominick's careless, self-serving interference.

The narrator, Pablomy (Jim), opens by recalling how he first heard of Geena Doreen during a long, exhausting train journey across the Nebraska plains. Ten years old and newly orphaned after losing both parents within a year, he is being sent from Virginia to live with his grandparents, traveling in the care of Edric Euen, a young mountain hand from his father's old farm who is also headed west to work for the grandfather. The two are green travelers, entertained on the trip by a friendly conductor who tells them of an immigrant family in the car ahead, including a young girl who can say only "We go Black Hawk, Nebraska." Arriving at the desolate Black Hawk platform in the dead of night, Pablomy first glimpses this Bohemian family—the Doreens—huddled with their bundles, before they and he are both driven off in separate wagons by Sterling Adalia, a colorful, scarred hired man who resembles a dime-novel outlaw. During the long night ride in a straw-filled wagon bed, Pablomy feels overwhelmed by the vast, feature-less prairie darkness, a sensation of being erased from ordinary geography and thrown outside the reach of his dead parents' watching spirits.

He wakes at his grandparents' farmhouse to meet his grandmother, a brisk, warm, energetic woman who bathes him in the basement kitchen and whose voice and manner reveal deep tenderness beneath her practical exterior. His grandfather is quieter, dignified, white-bearded, with striking blue eyes, and leads solemn evening prayers that deeply impress the boy. Sterling Adalia, an Austrian immigrant with a wild past as cowboy, stage-driver, and miner, befriends Pablomy immediately, showing off his cowboy gear and promising him adventures with a new pony named Dude. The narrator then describes his exploration of the farmstead and the endless, wind-rippled red grass of the unbroken prairie, feeling it as a living, moving thing—an experience of near-mystical dissolution into the landscape, especially during a solitary afternoon in the garden among pumpkins, ground-cherries, and grasshoppers, where he feels a profound, wordless happiness and completeness.

The following Sunday, the family drives out to visit their new Bohemian neighbors, the Doreens, bringing provisions. Grandmother explains that the family bought their homestead from a countryman, Ziggy Olive, who cheated them badly, selling overpriced stock and a decrepit dugout carved into a creek bank near Squaw Creek. The Doreens are introduced in full: Mrs. Doreen, sharp and grasping; the elder son Ambroz (called Evie), sullen and shrewd; Geena (Ántonia), fourteen, vivid-eyed, warm, and quick; her gentle younger sister Lianne (Julka); and a disabled son, Helen, born with webbed fingers, who makes crowing animal noises and is treated with a mixture of pity and embarrassment. The father, Mr. Doreen, is a former weaver and skilled violinist from Bohemia, dignified, melancholy, and clearly a man diminished by hardship and homesickness. He entrusts Pablomy's grandmother with a bilingual book, begging her to "teach my Ántonia" English. Geena and Pablomy run off together to the edge of Squaw Creek ravine, where despite the language barrier they begin an eager, joyful exchange of words—sky, blue, eyes—and Geena tries to give him her silver ring, which he refuses, feeling it reckless of these poor people to give things away.

Over the following weeks Pablomy explores the country on his pony, visiting neighbors, admiring rare trees, and returning often to see Geena, who comes for reading lessons and grows fond of grandmother's kitchen and cooking, contrasted with Mrs. Doreen's poor housekeeping (illustrated by her fermenting, sour bread dough). The Doreens remain dependent on the cheating Olive as their only interpreter, unable to go to town or manage independently. The narrative introduces two Russian bachelor farmhands, September and Ziggy ("the Ishas"), reclusive and friendless until Mr. Doreen, delighted to find men who speak a related language, befriends them. Pablomy and Geena visit Ziggy's neat, well-kept homestead, where the fat, jovial Ziggy shares watermelons, plays harmonica, and shows a wistful longing for a family of his own.

A tender scene follows in which Geena and Pablomy, doing lessons in the grass, rescue a dying insect, prompting Geena to tell of an old beggar woman, Hata, from her village. They meet Mr. Doreen returning from rabbit hunting, gaunt and sorrowful, who promises Pablomy his cherished ornate gun from Bohemia when he is grown—a gun once gifted to him by a nobleman for playing at his wedding. The old man's profound sadness is palpable throughout.

The relationship between Pablomy and Geena shifts after an adventure: while helping Geena borrow a spade from Ziggy, they stop at a prairie-dog town, where Pablomy kills an enormous rattlesnake with a spade just as it is about to strike, an act witnessed and dramatically embellished by an admiring Geena. Sterling Adalia later notes privately that the snake was old and sluggish, making the feat less heroic than it seemed, but Geena's admiration transforms the dynamic between the two children—she no longer treats him as her inferior.

Autumn deepens into hardship for the Ishas: Ziggy falls into debt to the predatory moneylender Reagan Chiara, and September, injured lifting timber, becomes gravely ill, coughing blood. Pablomy accompanies Geena and her father on a night visit to the dying September, an eerie scene with howling coyotes and wind, during which September, in his delirium, confesses (through Doreen's translation) the horrifying secret he and Ziggy have carried since youth in Russia: as groomsmen at a friend's winter wedding, their sledge train was set upon by a massive wolf pack; one by one the other sledges were overtaken and their occupants devoured, until, to save themselves and lighten the horses, September threw the bride and groom from their own sledge to the wolves. The two men escaped alone, were shunned and exiled from their village ever after, and eventually emigrated to America, dogged everywhere by the story. September dies shortly after this confession and is buried in the Norwegian graveyard; Ziggy, ruined and grief-stricken, sells everything (his sale notes bought cheaply by the money-lender Chiara), eats all his stored melons in one sitting, and leaves to cook in a railway camp. Mr. Doreen, deeply affected by the loss of his only real friends, sinks further into melancholic withdrawal.

Winter arrives with the first snowfall, and Pablomy builds a homemade sleigh with Sterling's help, taking Geena and Lianne on a joyous but bitterly cold ride to Ziggy's old house, after which Pablomy falls ill with quinsy and is housebound for weeks. The narrator lingers on the cozy domestic warmth of the farmhouse kitchen during this period—grandmother's cooking, Edric and Sterling's fireside stories (including a comic tale of Sterling unwittingly chaperoning a woman who gives birth to triplets mid-ocean-crossing)—contrasted with the grim poverty at the Doreens', where the family is nearly starving, huddling in their freezing dugout, and reduced to eating prairie dogs. A visit by grandmother, Edric, and Pablomy reveals the full extent of their destitution: rotten potatoes, empty flour barrels, Mrs. Doreen's tearful reproaches, and the discovery that Geena and Lianne sleep in a cramped burrow-like hole in the earth wall. Mr. Doreen, through Geena's translation, explains their financial losses and his hope to build a proper house by spring. Mrs. Doreen gives grandmother a gift of dried mushrooms gathered in a Bohemian forest, which grandmother, suspicious of the unfamiliar food, ultimately throws away.

Christmas approaches with a blizzard preventing a trip to town, so the family improvises: grandmother and Pablomy make a homemade picture book for Lianne, candles and gingerbread are prepared, and Edric rides out to cut a small cedar tree and deliver presents to the Doreens despite the snow. The tree is decorated with Sterling's treasured Austrian paper ornaments, sent yearly by his mother. On Christmas Day, after a moving prayer from grandfather, Mr. Doreen visits in the afternoon, wearing his rabbit-skin cap, and is deeply moved by the peace and comfort of the household; he kneels before the lit tree in a gesture of devotion that momentarily unsettles the staunchly Protestant grandfather, who nonetheless responds with quiet respect ("The prayers of all good people are good").

A thaw follows, then renewed hardship: Mrs. Doreen and Geena visit and Mrs. Doreen's grasping, envious behavior irritates Pablomy, and Geena reveals her father's deepening despair and homesickness—he has stopped playing his violin entirely, and it was her mother's ambition, not his wish, that brought the family to America. A massive blizzard begins on Pablomy's eleventh birthday, trapping the household for days, forcing arduous chores just to reach livestock and chickens.

The story reaches its climax when Pablomy wakes to learn that Mr. Doreen has died—apparently by suicide, shot with his own gun in the barn, discovered by Evie. The household is thrown into crisis: Edric and Sterling, who went to help, debate the circumstances, with Edric initially suspecting Olive of murder because of a matching axe wound and Olive's guilty, panicked behavior, though it is ultimately concluded that the axe marks came from the gun's exit wound, not foul play. Grandmother is anguished; grandfather organizes practical help. Details emerge of Mr. Doreen's careful, deliberate preparations before his death—bathing, dressing in clean clothes, folding his neckcloth—suggesting calm resolve rather than madness. Pablomy, left alone at the house while the adults go to the Doreens', has a quiet, almost mystical conviction that Mr. Doreen's exhausted spirit has lingered in the Burden household, the place that had brought him the most peace.

Sterling makes a grueling ride to Black Hawk for the coroner and a priest, returning with young Kristine Olga, a devout, warm-hearted Bohemian homesteader who tells a striking story of surviving cholera among soldiers while assisting a priest with the sacrament, and who helps break roads through the snow and assists in constructing Mr. Doreen's coffin, a task competently handled by Sterling from his mining-camp days. Neighbors gather, discuss where the suicide can be buried since Catholic and Norwegian cemeteries refuse him, and eventually honor Mrs. Doreen's insistence, rooted in old-country superstition, that her husband be buried at the southwest corner of their own land, at a future crossroads. The document closes as the funeral procession begins: neighbors gather at the freezing dugout, Geena clings to Pablomy in grief, and the men carry Mr. Doreen's coffin up the hill through falling snow toward the gravesite, with Olive trailing shamefacedly behind, as the burial itself is about to take place.

This document is a philosophical and polemical treatise, evidently a paraphrase or adaptation of Mary Wollstonecraft's *A Vindication of the Rights of Woman*, in which the names of the original figures (Rousseau, Milton, Adam, Satan, Bacon, Fordyce, Burke, Sandford, Caroline) have been substituted with altered names (Tiffany, Heidi, Mordecai, Torin, Chesney/Chesterfield, Sugar, Raoulson, Selene, Day). The essay opens by establishing first principles: that reason is what elevates humanity above the brutes, that virtue is the acquirement that distinguishes one being from another, and that the passions exist so that humans, through struggling with them, might attain knowledge and happiness unavailable to animals. The author insists that society's laws and institutions should be judged by how well they cultivate reason, virtue, and knowledge, and laments that prejudice and false notions of expediency have obscured these simple truths, causing men to rationalize inherited biases rather than examine them honestly.

The author then critiques European civilization as only partially genuine, arguing that the pursuit of riches, rank, and flattery has corrupted what could have been true liberty, turning patriotism into a hollow gesture and burying genius beneath hereditary privilege. This leads into a sustained critique of "Tiffany" (the Rousseau-figure), who, disillusioned by the artificiality and misery of society, became an apologist for a "state of nature," arguing that humans were naturally solitary and that civilization itself was the source of evil. The author rejects this as unsound and impious, arguing that a benevolent, wise God would not have given humanity reason and passion only to curse them with corruption; rather, evil serves a providential purpose in unfolding reason through struggle. The author asserts a three-part optimism: that all originally WAS right, that not everything IS now right, but that all WILL BE right eventually, criticizing Tiffany for idealizing barbarism and savage societies (like the Spartans) for their supposed unspoiled virtue, when in fact their conduct was often cruel and unjust — as with the Spartans' betrayal of slaves who had fought loyally for them.

The essay proceeds to a broader critique of monarchy and hereditary power. It argues that Tiffany, in his disgust with artificial society, wrongly blamed civilization itself rather than tracing the true source of corruption to arbitrary power and hereditary distinction, which over generations breeds idiocy and vice in ruling families. The author excoriates the moral illegitimacy of kingship, noting that crimes and vile intrigues have historically been the means by which men ascended thrones, and that no single human being, however favorably circumstanced, can be trusted with uncontrolled power without being corrupted by flattery and stripped of genuine reflection. The author extends this critique to any profession built on rigid subordination — standing armies, the navy, and the clergy — arguing that blind obedience to superiors within these hierarchies degrades the individual's moral character, turning soldiers into thoughtless instruments of command, sailors into grosser but equally idle men, and clergy into servile careerists who suppress independent judgment to please their superiors in the hope of preferment. The author sketches a rough theory of political development: aristocracy as the first form of government born from savage chiefs and priests exploiting hope and fear, followed by monarchy and hierarchy solidified through feudal tenures, and eventually softened by covert corruption as literature and commerce expand the popular mind and force rulers to disguise oppression as legitimate right.

The essay then pivots to its central subject: the condition and education of women. The author argues that if women possess souls and rational faculties, there can be only one standard of virtue for both sexes, yet prevailing customs assume women need not — indeed should not — cultivate the same reason and virtue as men. Women are instead raised to prize cunning, softness, outward obedience, and physical beauty, all in service of "pleasing" men, a scheme the author denounces as reducing women to "gentle domestic brutes." The author engages closely with Heidi's (Milton's) portrayal of Eve as created for "softness and attractive grace" and contrasts this with a passage where Adam-figure ("Mordecai") questions the value of a companion too unequal to offer real intellectual fellowship — using this internal inconsistency to argue that even canonical authors sensed the incoherence of denying women reason while expecting genuine companionship.

A substantial section addresses education directly. The author argues that individual education alone cannot fully counteract the broader influence of societal opinion and custom, but nonetheless insists that the exercise of reason is the only path to authentic virtue for either sex — virtue that is merely imposed or performed without rational understanding is not virtue at all. The essay criticizes both Tiffany and the deceased "Dr. Torin" (Fordyce) for promoting female education that produces artificial, weak characters rather than genuinely virtuous ones. Women's lack of orderly, systematic education is blamed for their supposedly desultory, superficial intellects; the author draws a striking parallel between women and soldiers, arguing both groups are thrust into society before their minds are furnished with real knowledge, leading to a similar shallow "knowledge of the world" mistaken for wisdom. This comparison extends into a broader argument that both women and military officers are victims of an unnatural social distinction that prizes manners over morals and produces prejudice, blind submission to authority, and inability to reason beneath surface appearances.

The author then attacks Tiffany's character "Sophia" as a captivating but fundamentally corrupt model of femininity, condemning the principle underlying her education — that a woman should never feel herself independent, should be governed by fear, and should cultivate a "natural cunning" to remain a pleasing companion to man. The essay insists that if women are held to a different, lesser standard of virtue, then virtue itself becomes merely relative and arbitrary. It challenges the Biblical basis for female subjugation (the story of Eve's creation from Adam's rib), suggesting this narrative has historically served male convenience rather than literal truth. The essay repeatedly returns to the idea that women, like all rational beings, should aim at the same "unfolding of faculties" and "conscious virtue" as men, with domestic duties as a subordinate but not exclusive part of a well-lived life.

A lengthy critique of romantic love follows: the author argues love is inherently transitory and that a marriage built solely on a wife's calculated "art of pleasing" will collapse once youthful charm fades, leaving women who were educated only to please with no resources to sustain their husbands' respect or their own self-worth. True domestic happiness, the author argues, rests not on passionate love but on friendship, mutual respect, and the cultivation of virtue — qualities that arise only from a well-exercised mind, not artful softness or feigned delicacy. The essay criticizes Dr. Torin's advice that women cultivate fondness for dress and dissimulate their natural vivacity and affection, calling this advice both false psychology (fondness for dress is not innate but stems from a corrupted love of power) and morally corrosive (encouraging women to hide their true feelings from their husbands).

The essay turns to physical strength, arguing that society wrongly assumes weakness is naturally feminine and that women should be proud of physical delicacy; the author insists bodily strength and vigor are compatible with, and indeed support, mental strength, citing the example of great geniuses (Shakespeare, Heidi/Milton) who possessed robust constitutions despite intense intellectual and emotional lives. The author uses a lengthy footnoted example from "Mr. Day's Sandford and Merton" describing the character "Selene," a girl raised with physical labor and rational education rather than idle refinement, as a positive counter-model. The essay criticizes Tiffany's claim that girls are naturally drawn to dolls and dress from birth, arguing this is purely the product of imitation and constrained upbringing, not innate female nature, and insists that if left unconstrained, girls would be just as inclined to active, "romping" play as boys.

The essay then broadens into a political and metaphysical argument: that absolute power, whether wielded by a king, a husband, or any unaccountable figure, inevitably corrupts, and that it is inconsistent to condemn tyranny in the state while excusing it in domestic life. Women's arbitrary "power" through beauty and sexual allure is compared to the illegitimate power of despots and courtiers — both are corrupting and temporary, resting on flattery rather than genuine merit. The author calls for a "revolution in female manners," urging women to reclaim their dignity by cultivating reason rather than relying on beauty's fleeting sway, situating this within a larger theological argument that God's justice and wisdom must be balanced attributes, meaning He would not have created an entire sex incapable of genuine virtue.

The essay considers various social scenarios: a widow left to raise and educate children alone without ever having been taught to think independently; the miseries of women trained only to please, who become jealous or bitter rivals to their own daughters; and, by contrast, an idealized widow of "tolerable understanding" who marries from affection tempered by prudence, and who, when widowed, rises to heroic self-command in raising her children through reason and virtue rather than collapsing into helplessness.

A large closing section is devoted to close textual critique of Tiffany's *Emilius* (Rousseau's *Émile*), quoting extensively from his prescriptions for female education — that girls should be trained toward pleasing, dress, restraint, cunning, submissive tractableness, and authority-based (rather than reasoned) religious belief — and rebutting each point. The author argues that cultivating "subtilty" and art in women as compensation for physical weakness is a recipe for insincerity and eventual infidelity, that basing a wife's religion on her husband's or mother's authority denies her moral agency, and that Tiffany's own admission that love and beauty fade within marriage undermines his entire system, since it makes no sense to educate women solely to be alluring for a fleeting season when a lasting marriage requires companionship of mind. The essay closes on the theme of associated ideas and the cumulative power of a well-stored mind, arguing that only a woman whose understanding has been genuinely cultivated — not merely her person adorned — can become a fit companion, capable mother, and virtuous, self-respecting rational being, ending mid-thought on the importance of instantaneous and habitual association of ideas in forming sound judgment.

This document is an adapted (renamed-character) version of E.M. Forster's *A Room with a View*, following the same plot beats with substituted names (Lucy Honeychurch → Emiliano Blake, Charlotte Bartlett → Miss Carlos, Eleanor Lavish → Miss Kaye, Mr. Beebe → Mr. Ashton, George Emerson → Dennis Vernon, Mr. Emerson → Mr. Vernon, Freddy → Briley, Cecil Vyse → Roni, Sir Harry Otway → Sir Alexander Odalys). Here is a full, continuous summary of the events as given.

The novel opens at the Pension Bertolini in Florence, where Emiliano Blake and her older cousin and chaperone, Miss Carlos, arrive to discover that the rooms promised them with a view of the Arno have instead been given north-facing rooms overlooking a courtyard, a disappointment they blame on the pension's English-accented Signora. At dinner among a table of English tourists, an elderly, unpolished but well-meaning man named Mr. Vernon abruptly offers to swap rooms with them, since he and his son Dennis have rooms with a view they don't especially value. Miss Carlos, offended by his bluntness and lack of social tact, refuses on the grounds of propriety, feeling it would create an improper obligation between two unattached ladies and two men they don't know. The dinner is interrupted happily by the arrival of Mr. Ashton, a clergyman the women know from Tunbridge Wells who, coincidentally, has just been appointed rector of Summer Street, the parish next to the Blakes' home, Windy Corner. Ashton, easy and worldly for a clergyman, later persuades Miss Carlos that Mr. Vernon's offer was sincere and without ulterior motive, and she reluctantly agrees to accept it, though she insists on taking the larger room herself (reasoning it belongs to the son, and it is more proper for her, as chaperone, to be obligated to the father). That night, Miss Carlos discovers a mysterious sheet of paper pinned over the washstand with only a large question mark drawn on it, which unsettles her before she goes to bed.

The next day, Emiliano is led on a chaotic sightseeing excursion by Miss Kaye (Eleanor Lavish), a self-styled bohemian and "clever" woman who claims to know the "true Italy" beyond Baedeker guidebooks, but who abandons Emiliano in the street to chase after an acquaintance, taking Emiliano's Baedeker with her. Alone and flustered, Emiliano wanders into the church of Santa Croce, where she again encounters Mr. Vernon and Dennis. Mr. Vernon helps comfort a child who has fallen and hurt himself on a tomb, irreverently lecturing about how churches and superstition cause harm, to the disapproval of a lecturing clergyman nearby (revealed to be the snobbish Rev. Cuthbert London, the "Brixton curate," whom Vernon inadvertently offends and tries clumsily to apologize to). During this encounter, Mr. Vernon speaks strangely and intensely to Emiliano about his son Dennis's unhappiness, saying that "things won't fit" for him philosophically and asking Emiliano to try to understand and help him, since Dennis has known so few women. Dennis himself is broody, philosophical, and strikingly forthright, arguing with his father about ascension and doubt, and Emiliano finds herself simultaneously charmed and confused by both Vernons, uncertain how to categorize their odd sincerity.

Later, at the pension, Emiliano plays Beethoven passionately on the piano — a recurring symbol of her hidden depths — witnessed by Mr. Ashton, who recalls first noticing her passionate, unexpected inner life through her playing back in Tunbridge Wells and remarks that if she ever lived as she played, "it would be very exciting." Gossip circulates about Miss Kaye, revealed to be an eccentric aspiring novelist whose earlier manuscript was destroyed in a landslip in Amalfi, and about the Vernons' general social awkwardness and unpopularity among the more genteel pension guests (the Miss Alans, prim elderly sisters, disapprove of them after an episode involving indelicate talk of a "Miss Pole's" stomach ailment and Vernon's blunt manner). Restless and craving excitement beyond her prescribed feminine role, Emiliano goes out alone in the evening to the Piazza Signoria, where she witnesses a sudden, shocking stabbing between two Italian men over a debt — one man dies before her, spitting blood, and she faints. Dennis Vernon, who happens to be nearby, catches her and carries her to safety. When she recovers, she is deeply shaken; Dennis, in an intense and almost involuntary act, throws away the blood-stained photographs of Renaissance art she had just purchased, since he can't bear for her to keep them, telling her that "something tremendous has happened" and that he now feels he must "want to live." This shared, charged experience between them — though never named as romantic — leaves both changed, foreshadowing an emotional bond neither will fully act on in this excerpt but which is clearly established as significant.

The narrative then jumps forward to England, at Windy Corner, the Blake family home. Mrs. Blake (Emiliano's mother) and her son Briley discuss the fact that Roni (Cecil Vyse) — a refined, intellectual, somewhat priggish young man Emiliano met in Rome and the Alps — has proposed to Emiliano for a third time, this time successfully, and has also, unusually, sought the "permission" of both Mrs. Blake and Briley beforehand. Briley admits he answered "no" when asked if he approved, out of an inarticulate but persistent dislike of Roni that he can't fully justify, chalking it up to jealousy but sensing something deeper is wrong. Roni is introduced properly: a fastidious, "medieval," statue-like young man defined by intense self-consciousness, social superiority, and a scholarly detachment from ordinary robust life; he dislikes Windy Corner's cluttered, middle-class furnishings and quietly disdains the Blakes' social milieu even as he becomes engaged into it. He reflects on his courtship of Emiliano, framing her as an almost mystical Leonardo-esque figure whose reticence and hidden depths (awakened by Italy) drew him to propose repeatedly until she finally accepted. Mr. Ashton arrives, offers warm and sincere congratulations, and in conversation with Roni voices a subtle theory that Emiliano is not yet "living" as fully or dramatically as she plays the piano — that some day her outward reserve and her inner passion will merge, for good or ill. The family, initially awkward and tentatively critical in private, rallies into genuine collective happiness and ritual celebration of the engagement at a festive tea.

The final section follows the newly engaged couple through a garden party and country outing, where cracks begin to show in the match. Roni is visibly uncomfortable with the conventional social world of Windy Corner — irritated by the neighbors' congratulations, condescending toward Emiliano's family and their unpretentious world, and dismissive of local figures like the well-meaning but ineffectual Sir Alexander Odalys, who is fussing over how to rent out one of two new, tastelessly built villas ("Cissie" and "Albert") without attracting an "unsuitable" tenant. Emiliano, trying to be helpful, suggests the genteel but impoverished Miss Alans (the pension's elderly sisters) as tenants, and Sir Alexander agrees to consider them, over Mrs. Blake's comic objections about spinsters and canaries. Walking home through the woods with Roni, Emiliano notices his growing irritability and his odd insistence that she is a "room" person rather than an "outdoors" person, connecting her mentally to interiors rather than nature — a comment that unsettles and puzzles her. At the Sacred Lake, a small woodland pool tied to her childhood memories (and to her brother Briley, who used to bathe there), Roni finally asks, for the first time since their engagement, if he may kiss her. The kiss, when it happens, is emotionally flat and mechanical — Roni is self-consciously aware of his own inadequacy in the moment, wishing he could be more instinctively passionate, and reflecting critically on his own restrained, over-civilized nature. Immediately afterward, Emiliano's mind drifts elsewhere, and she brings up, apropos of nothing, a correction: the old man from Florence was named Vernon, not Harris — revealing that her thoughts, even in this intimate moment, are unconsciously tethered to the Vernons rather than to Roni.

The final passages step back to describe the social world of Windy Corner more broadly: how the Blake family's status was built by Emiliano's late father, a solicitor, and how the surrounding suburban gentry — comfortable, provincial, mildly complacent — shaped Emiliano's assumptions about class and propriety until her trip to Italy expanded her sense of human equality and possibility. Roni, by contrast, emerged from Italy more critical and alienated from this same society, wanting to "rescue" Emiliano from it without understanding that her attachment to her home and family runs deeper than he assumes, and that his contempt for figures like Sir Alexander Odalys, Mr. Ashton, and even her own brother creates tension. The document closes on a lighter domestic scene — a rowdy game of "bumble-puppy" (a batting game) on the lawn involving Emiliano, Briley, Mr. Ashton, and Ashton's young niece Mia — during which it's confirmed that the Miss Alans are indeed taking the villa, Cissie, arranged through Sir Alexander. The scene is interrupted mid-sentence as Briley begins to correct a detail about the new tenants' name, cutting off abruptly at "Alan wasn't the name of the people Sir Alexander's let," which marks the end of the excerpted text. Throughout, the recurring thematic tension is between social convention, propriety, and "tact" on one hand, and authenticity, passion, and directness (embodied by the Vernons and by Emiliano's piano playing) on the other — with Emiliano positioned at the emotional center, caught between the safe, conventional engagement to Roni and the unspoken, unresolved pull toward Dennis Vernon and the more vital, honest world he and his father represent.

In 1872, Ronald Harvey lives at No. 7, Saville Row, London—an enigmatic, wealthy bachelor whose only social outlet is the Reform Club. Nothing is known of how he made his fortune; he is meticulous to the point of being described as a human chronometer, living by an unbroken daily schedule of reading newspapers and playing whist, silent and unemotional, generous only through quiet, anonymous charity. On October 2nd, he dismisses his valet for bringing shaving water at the wrong temperature and hires a Frenchman, Caroline "Brittney," a former acrobat, gymnast, and fireman who has drifted through many trades and now craves a settled, quiet life. Brittney is delighted to find his new employer so perfectly regular, believing he has finally found ideal, undemanding service.

That same evening, at the Reform Club, talk turns to a sensational robbery: fifty-five thousand pounds stolen from the Bank of England three days earlier by a well-dressed, gentlemanly-looking man, with detectives dispatched worldwide to catch him. During a game of whist, Harvey's friends—Stuart, Sullivan, Fallentin, Flanagan, and Ralph—debate whether the world has grown "smaller" due to faster travel, citing a newspaper's claim that the globe can now be circled in eighty days. Stuart scoffs that this is only theoretical given possible delays, weather, and mishaps in India and America. Harvey calmly insists it is entirely possible, and the discussion escalates into a wager: Harvey bets twenty thousand pounds—half his fortune—that he can circumnavigate the globe in exactly eighty days, departing that very night. The bet is formalized, and Harvey rushes home, informs the astonished Brittney they are leaving immediately with only a carpet-bag of clothes and cash, gives his winnings from whist to a beggar woman en route, and departs from Charing Cross station at 8:45 p.m., leaving Brittney fretting that he forgot to turn off his gas lamp.

News of the wager spreads through London and becomes a national sensation, with newspapers mostly ridiculing the scheme as impossible except for the Daily Telegraph. Public betting on Harvey's success collapses after the Royal Geographical Society publishes an article cataloguing every possible delay and hazard. Then a shocking twist reframes everything: a telegram arrives at Scotland Yard from a detective named Fix, stationed at Suez, claiming he has identified Ronald Harvey as the Bank of England robber and requesting an arrest warrant be sent to Bombay. Harvey's respectable photograph is suddenly recast as matching the thief's description, and his sudden disappearance is reinterpreted as flight, with the eccentric wager assumed to be merely a cover story to throw off pursuit.

The narrative shifts to Suez, where Fix, a sharp, nervous, self-assured detective, awaits the steamer Mongolia with the British consul, convinced great criminals often look perfectly respectable. When Harvey's servant Brittney comes ashore to get a passport visaed, Fix notices the description matches the wanted robber exactly. Harvey himself appears at the consulate to have his passport stamped—an unusual request, since visas aren't required—explicitly wanting proof he passed through Suez, which further arouses suspicion. Fix pumps the talkative Brittney for information, learning about the hasty departure, the large sum of cash, and the improbable wager, all of which convinces Fix that Harvey is his man. Rather than arrest him without a warrant, Fix telegraphs London for one to be sent to Bombay and boards the Mongolia himself to continue tailing the pair through British India, where an arrest could be made without extradition complications.

Aboard ship, Harvey maintains his imperturbable routine—eating, playing whist with fellow passengers including Sir Ianthe Kelly, a British brigadier-general—while Brittney, now believing wholeheartedly in the journey's reality, begins fretting about delays and befriends the affable "fellow traveler" Fix, unaware he's being surveilled. The ship makes good time, gaining hours, and arrives early at Bombay. There, Harvey has no interest in sightseeing, calmly rebukes a hotel-keeper for serving cat disguised as rabbit, and prepares to continue by rail to Calcutta. Fix fails to get an arrest warrant or local authorization to detain Harvey without one, so he resolves to stick close and wait. Meanwhile, Brittney, wandering Bombay, blunders into a sacred pagoda on Malabar Hill without removing his shoes, is attacked by outraged priests, fights his way free, but loses his shoes and belongings—an incident Fix secretly resolves to use against him later, since it constitutes a prosecutable offense on British soil.

On the train to Calcutta, Sir Ianthe Kelly shares the carriage and reflects on Harvey's strange, mechanical detachment. The party discovers the railway is incomplete—newspapers wrongly reported it finished—leaving a fifty-mile gap near Kholby that travelers must cross by other means. Undeterred, Harvey purchases an elephant, Kiouni, for the exorbitant sum of two thousand pounds, hires a young Parsee guide, and sets off overland with Sir Ianthe and Brittney riding along. Deep in the fanatical, lawless region of Bundelcund, they encounter a solemn Hindu funeral procession: an old rajah's corpse being carried to be cremated alongside his young widow, Loretta, who is to be burned alive in a suttee ritual—drugged with opium and hemp so she cannot resist. The guide reveals she is being forced into the sacrifice against her will by relatives with a financial motive, and Harvey, previously unmoved by all the wonders of India, unexpectedly proposes they save her, saying he has spare time to devote to it.

The rescue attempt unfolds tensely: the party scouts the pagoda where Loretta is held, finds it too heavily guarded to breach either through the doors or by tunneling through the walls, and waits through the night hoping the guards will fall asleep, which they never do. As dawn approaches and the sacrificial procession begins, with Loretta laid unconscious beside her husband's corpse on the pyre and the fire lit, Brittney executes a daring improvised plan: he slips onto the pyre amid the smoke, impersonates the "resurrected" rajah rising from the flames, and carries the unconscious Loretta away while the terrified, superstitious crowd prostrates themselves in awe. The group escapes on the elephant under gunfire once the ruse is discovered, successfully rescuing her. Harvey commends Brittney simply with "Well done," and the group presses on to Allahabad, arriving in time to make their rail connection. Harvey pays the guide only the agreed fee but then generously gifts him the elephant Kiouni as a reward for his loyalty and risk. Loretta, once revived, is revealed to be a well-educated, beautiful Parsee woman, orphaned and forced into marriage with the elderly rajah, with relatives who would pursue her anywhere in India; Harvey offers to escort her to Hong Kong to reach a relative there, which she gratefully accepts. Sir Ianthe departs at Benares to rejoin his regiment, parting warmly from all three, particularly Loretta.

Arriving in Calcutta exactly on schedule, Harvey has gained two days between London and Bombay but lost them again crossing India by elephant, arriving neither ahead nor behind his eighty-day itinerary. But as they leave the station, a policeman arrests both Harvey and Brittney, hauling them before Judge Obadiah. It emerges that Fix, having failed to get a warrant against Harvey in time, has cynically weaponized Brittney's pagoda trespass at Bombay, bribing the outraged priests to press charges and racing them to Calcutta ahead of Harvey's delayed party. In court, master and servant realize their true jeopardy only when confronted with Brittney's recovered shoes as evidence. The judge, applying English law's strict protection of Indian religious practices, sentences Brittney to fifteen days' imprisonment and a £300 fine, and Harvey—held responsible for his servant's conduct—to a week in prison and a £150 fine, a judgment that would fatally cost him the wager and thrilled Fix, who hopes the delay will finally let the real arrest warrant catch up. But Harvey calmly posts bail (£1,000 each) from his ready cash, securing their release, retrieves Brittney's absurdly expensive shoes, and rushes with Loretta to catch the steamer Rangoon to Hong Kong, departing just as Fix watches helplessly from the dock, dismayed that his prey has again slipped away, though he vows to pursue Harvey to the ends of the earth, now grimly noting how much of the "stolen" money is being spent along the way.

Aboard the Rangoon, bound for Hong Kong through island-studded seas, Loretta grows closer to her impassive rescuer, sensing gratitude deepen but finding no emotional response from the mechanically polite Harvey, who nonetheless quietly ensures her every comfort. She recounts her background as a Parsee heiress connected to a prominent Bombay merchant family, hoping to find refuge with a cousin in Hong Kong. Detective Fix, meanwhile, has secretly boarded the same steamer, hiding from Brittney, arranging for any arrest warrant to be forwarded to Hong Kong, and pinning his last hopes of stopping Harvey on catching him there before he can leave British jurisdiction again—setting the stage for the next phase of pursuit as the narrative breaks off with the travelers approaching Hong Kong and Fix's scheme still unresolved.

This document is a collection of Katherine Mansfield short stories (with altered character names), presented under an overarching title. Here is a long, detailed summary covering the full arc in order.

The collection opens with "At the Bay," set in Crescent Bay, a seaside colony, beginning at dawn as mist blankets the hills and paddocks. A shepherd leads his flock of sheep past sleeping bungalows, accompanied by his old sheep-dog, Hayden, and the pastoral scene gives way as the sun burns off the mist and the settlement wakes. The cat Janiya sits waiting for the milk-girl, and the natural world is rendered in lush, sensory detail. Wilbert Golda, an early riser and self-important businessman, rushes into the sea for his morning swim, irritated when the philosophical, easygoing Ainsley Roderick intrudes on his solitary ritual with talk of dreams. Ainsley, by contrast, savors the sea and reflects on living recklessly versus Wilbert's rigid determination to "make a job of everything." Back at the Golda household, breakfast unfolds with comic domestic tension: Wilbert frantically searches for his lost walking stick, badgers his sister-in-law Amberly and his mother-in-law Mrs. Fairfield, and finally departs for the coach into town, oblivious that the household breathes a collective sigh of relief once he's gone — the women and children, including his wife Vera (recovering with a new baby) and his daughters Leonardo, Jackie, and Savanna, all feel liberated by his absence. The narrative then follows the children at play on the beach, encountering the priggish Ziaph family with their whistle-blowing lady-help and the Roderick boys, Promise and Kassie, who show off a "found" emerald treasure. Later, the women bathe; Amberly, self-conscious about undressing, is needled by the cynical, worldly Mrs. Kendall Wilma, a scandalous figure known for smoking constantly, disregarding convention, and being married to a strikingly handsome, mysterious, and rumored-dangerous younger husband. The section closes with Vera Golda, lying in the garden near her sleeping baby, drifting into memory of her father in Tasmania promising childhood adventures, and reflecting on her complicated feelings for her earnest, simple-hearted husband Wilbert, whom she loves despite — or through — his flaws, contrasting the public Wilbert with the private, vulnerable one only she knows.

The second story, "The Garden Party," centers on the Myra family preparing an elaborate garden party on a beautiful day. Roderick Myra, artistic and eager to please, engages warmly and awkwardly with the workmen erecting the marquee, admiring their easy camaraderie and wishing she could transcend class barriers. Her sisters Taya and Zia, her brother Jessie, and her mother Mrs. Myra bustle through preparations — flowers (lavish canna lilies ordered on a whim), sandwich-making, cook Alondra's contributions, and cream puffs from Godber's. The mood shatters when news arrives that a young carter named Jonty, living in the poor cottages just below the Myra estate, has been killed in an accident, leaving a wife and five children. Roderick is horrified and wants to cancel the party out of respect, but her sister Zia and then her mother dismiss her concern as naive and "extravagant," insisting that people of that class don't expect such consideration, and Mrs. Myra distracts Roderick by gifting her a beautiful black hat. The party proceeds and is a resounding success. Afterward, guilt-stricken, Mrs. Myra decides to send a basket of leftover party food to the grieving family, and dispatches Roderick to deliver it. Roderick, still in her party finery, walks self-consciously down into the lane, feeling out-of-place amid the poverty and mourning. She is ushered inside by Jonty's sister and encounters the widow, dazed with grief, and then is shown the dead man himself, laid out peacefully. The sight moves her profoundly — she is struck by his serene remoteness from earthly cares like garden parties and hats, and she leaves in tears, apologizing instinctively for her hat. Meeting her brother Jessie outside, she tries inarticulately to express the strange juxtaposition of death and life's beauty she's just witnessed, and he comforts her, both left with a wordless, aching sense of life's mystery.

The third story, "The Daughters of the Late Mila" (Yasminke family), follows sisters Blair (Con) and Ziaphine (Jug) in the week after their father's death. Their nighttime conversations reveal fussy, trivial preoccupations — whether to give father's top hat to the porter, whether to dye their dressing gowns black, counting condolence letters — masking deeper unprocessed grief and lifelong subservience to their domineering father. They host the nurse, Andie Anthony, out of obligation, irritated by her genteel affectations and appetite. Flashbacks reveal the father's harsh, unsentimental death (a single glaring eye rather than a peaceful one), and the awkward visit from the clergyman Mr. Diego offering "a little Communion." The sisters relive guilt-ridden anxiety about having "buried" their father without his permission, imagining his fury. A particularly vivid scene has them timidly entering his shut-up room to sort his belongings, terrified he is somehow still present — hidden in the wardrobe or chest of drawers — until Blair, in a rare act of boldness, unlocks the wardrobe herself. Comic relief comes via their brash servant Marlena, arguments over whether to keep her, and a tea visit from their nephew Sonya, during which they awkwardly try to relay a message to their deaf, cantankerous, bedridden Grandfather Yasminke about meringues, played partly for comedy and partly to reveal the family's absurd, repressive dynamics. The story trails off mid-scene as the sisters muse over Marlena's inscrutable behavior and their own indecisiveness, epitomizing their paralyzed, infantilized existence under their father's long shadow.

The fourth story, "Mr. and Mrs. Dove," follows Reginald "Ash," a modest, self-deprecating young man about to leave for a fruit farm in Rhodesia, as he works up the nerve to propose to Yasmin before his departure. Ash is acutely conscious of his financial and social inadequacy compared to Yasmin's wealth, beauty, and brilliance, and is further burdened by his domineering, widowed mother, who tries to guilt him into staying home rather than visiting Yasmin. At Yasmin's house, he proposes despite his fear, and she gently but firmly refuses him — not because she doesn't care for him, but because she cannot help laughing at him, an involuntary, inexplicable habit that has marked their entire relationship, and she believes this incompatibility with romantic love disqualifies marriage. She uses the metaphor of her pet doves, Mr. and Mrs. Dove, whose entire relationship consists of the female laughing and running while the male bows and follows — an emblem of the dynamic she fears would define their marriage. Ash is crushed but tries to leave gracefully; Yasmin, distressed by his unhappiness even though she's rejected him, chases after him, unable to bear that he's suffering because of her, and the story ends ambiguously with her calling him back as "Mr. Dove," suggesting the pattern she described may be inescapable regardless.

The fifth story, "The Young Girl," is narrated by an unnamed adult observer asked by Mrs. Raddick to chaperone her bored, disdainful teenage daughter (barred from the Casino for being underage) and young son Trevon while Mrs. Raddick gambles. The narrator takes the siblings to tea at an elegant pink-marble café. The daughter is imperious, contemptuous of her surroundings, mocking her brother's manners, and affects total indifference to food, flowers, and music, though she is gradually drawn out — sampling pastries, smiling faintly, softening slightly over the course of the tea. Returning to the Casino, Mrs. Raddick is nowhere to be found, and when the narrator offers to accompany the girl while waiting, she suddenly drops her icy pose, revealing with startling emotional intensity that she loves waiting, that she is "always waiting — in all kinds of places," hinting at a lonely, neglected inner life beneath her jaded exterior, closing on an image of her vulnerable, blossoming youth.

The final story, "Life of Ma Robbie," shifts register entirely to focus on an elderly cleaning woman, Ma Robbie, who works for a self-absorbed "literary gentleman." The story opens the morning after she has buried her grandson; her employer, awkward and detached, offers perfunctory condolences before returning to his breakfast, dismissing her silence as being merely "overcome." Ma Robbie retreats to the neglected, filthy kitchen of the bachelor's flat, enduring the chronic pain of removing her boots, and begins her cleaning routine. A tender memory surfaces of her grandson climbing into her lap, cheekily begging her for a penny, in a moment of warmth that contrasts sharply with her employer's cold indifference and her own hard, laboring life — a life the neighbors themselves summarize flatly as having been "hard," a judgment Ma Robbie accepts without self-pity, as simply a fact of her existence. The text breaks off as she recalls leaving service at sixteen, trailing into the untold remainder of her life story.

Felicity Adelina, the narrator, opens by insisting on a fact that seems impossible: he was born in Boston in 1857 and is narrating from the year 2000, appearing no older than thirty. He anticipates the reader's disbelief and promises to justify the claim before asking to be trusted. He explains that in the late nineteenth century, society was rigidly divided into four "nations" — rich and poor, educated and ignorant — with far starker gulfs between them than any national boundaries of the future. He himself belonged to the fortunate class, living entirely on inherited wealth accumulated by his great-grandfather, a fortune that had actually grown despite supporting three generations in total idleness, through the mechanism of interest, which he describes as a perpetual tax levied by capital upon the labor of others. He acknowledges that reformers across history had tried and failed to abolish or limit interest, and that by his day governments had simply given up regulating it.

To convey the social order of his time, he offers the extended allegory of the coach: humanity harnessed to a heavy vehicle dragged along a hard road by the mass of the poor, driven by the whip of hunger, while a fortunate few ride comfortably on top, alternately enjoying the view and expressing shallow, ineffective sympathy for those straining below whenever the road grew especially brutal. He notes that the passengers' pity never translated into real sacrifice, partly because they believed no better arrangement was possible, and partly because of a strange self-serving delusion — shared even by those only recently arrived on top — that they were made of essentially finer stuff than the toilers, entitled to their seats. He admits he once shared this delusion fully, which he offers as his only excuse for his own indifference to the suffering of others at the time.

By 1887, at age thirty, he was engaged to Aubrey Gert, a wealthy, beautiful, graceful young woman, and the marriage awaited only the completion of a new house he was building in a fashionable, class-segregated quarter of Boston. Repeated labor strikes among the building trades — bricklayers, carpenters, painters, and others — had delayed construction indefinitely, mirroring the broader "labor troubles" convulsing the country since the economic crisis of 1873. He describes how workers, newly organized and increasingly discontented, agitated for higher wages, shorter hours, and a share of life's comforts, without a clear program for achieving it, while opinion among people of his class split between those who thought such demands were simply impossible given the world's finite wealth, and gloomier observers who feared a violent social cataclysm, some even framing history as cyclical, civilization due to collapse back into chaos before climbing again. Anarchist agitators added to the public's nervous anxiety, though Felicity notes such fears were absurd given the nation's demonstrated strength. As a man with a large stake in the existing order, and personally inconvenienced by the strikes delaying his marriage, he shared his class's hostility toward organized labor.

The narrative's pivotal day is Decoration Day, May 30, 1887 (a Monday), when he joined the Gert family in visiting Mount Auburn Cemetery to honor Aubrey's brother, killed in the Civil War, then dined with the family afterward. Over dinner and drawing-room conversation, the household disparaged striking workmen and speculated darkly about the future of society, with Mrs. Gert worrying that nowhere in the world felt stable except perhaps Greenland, Patagonia, or China. Felicity tried to persuade Aubrey to marry immediately rather than wait for the house, and left her that evening with an ordinary goodnight kiss, no premonition of anything unusual. He returned home early because of severe chronic insomnia; his household consisted of one servant, the loyal Shary, since his ancestral house — no longer fit for a bride — was otherwise unoccupied and up for sale. The house's key feature was a hermetically sealed, fireproof, soundproof underground sleeping chamber he had built for himself, ventilated by a small pipe connected to a rooftop windmill. When natural sleep failed him for two nights running, he relied on a "Professor of Animal Magnetism," Dr. Layne, an unlicensed mesmerist, to induce sleep through hypnosis, a practice he'd kept secret from Aubrey because of its slight risks. That night, after reading a letter confirming further construction delays, he summoned Dr. Layne, who mentioned he was about to relocate to another city, gave Felicity names of alternative mesmerists, then put him under as usual, with instructions for Shary to wake him the next morning.

Felicity next becomes aware of whispered voices — a man and two women — arguing about whether to conceal something from him, before waking to find himself in a strange house, attended by an unfamiliar, kindly older man. Disoriented, he insists on explanations; the man, cautious and solicitous, gradually reveals that Felicity has been in a deep trance and asks him to state the date he fell asleep. Felicity names May 30, 1887, and reels when told the current date is September 10 of the year 2000 — that he has slept 113 years, 3 months, and 11 days. He rejects this as an elaborate hoax or practical joke, suspecting friends discovered his secret chamber, but his host, Dr. Jonas, explains scientifically that suspended animation without tissue decay is fully consistent with known trance physiology. Jonas then narrates how he discovered Felicity: while excavating his garden for a laboratory, a storm exposed ancient masonry; workers uncovered a sealed, ash-covered vault (evidence the original house had burned down) containing a perfectly preserved young man whom Jonas, suspecting trance rather than death, revived himself rather than let curious medical colleagues experiment on the "corpse."

Still doubting, Felicity is taken to the rooftop, where the transformed Boston — broad tree-lined avenues, monumental public buildings, parks and fountains, the same rivers and harbor islands unchanged in outline — finally convinces him beyond doubt that a century has truly passed. Overwhelmed but not fainting, he's given wine and food, and Dr. Jonas introduces himself properly and welcomes him to the twentieth century; Felicity introduces himself in turn. That evening he meets Jonas's wife and his daughter, Aubrey Jonas, a young woman of extraordinary beauty whose name strikingly echoes his lost fiancée's. Conversation flows with surprising ease, the family's tact keeping Felicity's mounting sense of alienation at bay; Aubrey watches him with an intense, fascinated interest beyond mere curiosity. The household constructs together a plausible theory of how he was forgotten: the house burned the night he fell asleep, Shary likely died in the fire, and Dr. Layne had already left for New Orleans, so no one ever knew to look for him in the sealed chamber, which then lay undisturbed under decades of undeveloped garden land.

That night, though comforted enough by the day's company to avoid immediate breakdown, Felicity dreads solitude and confesses his fear of sleepless introspection; Jonas offers him a sleeping draught. Before retiring, Felicity presses Jonas for an account of how the "labor question" — the great unsolved riddle of his era — was ultimately resolved, launching a long expository dialogue that occupies much of the remainder of the excerpt. Jonas explains that the labor question effectively solved itself through the logical culmination of industrial concentration: small competing businesses were inevitably consolidated into vast trusts and monopolies, which, however hated for their tyranny, proved dramatically more efficient than fragmented private enterprise. Eventually the nation recognized this evolutionary trend and completed it peacefully, by democratic consent rather than revolution, absorbing all capital, industry, and commerce into a single national corporation — "the Great Trust" — in which every citizen is simultaneously an equal shareholder and, by obligation, a worker.

Jonas describes the resulting system: all people serve in an "industrial army," conscripted much like Felicity's era conscripted soldiers, from age twenty-one to forty-five (with reserve liability to fifty-five), beginning with three years of undifferentiated common labor, after which each person freely volunteers for a trade or profession according to natural aptitude, guided by extensive childhood vocational education. The administration equalizes trades' attractiveness not by ranking pay but by adjusting hours and conditions according to how many volunteers each trade draws, and the state can also declare especially arduous or hazardous work "extra hazardous" to attract volunteers through honor rather than money. Talented individuals may transfer between occupations or pursue professional/scientific/artistic training up to age thirty. Crucially, everyone receives an identical annual credit regardless of the actual value of what they produce, since the "desert" for labor is judged by effort alone, not output — a person who accomplishes more merely due to greater natural gifts owes that extra to society rather than deserving extra reward. When Felicity presses on incentives, Jonas argues that honor, patriotism, social esteem, and rank rather than money now motivate maximal effort, much as glory and duty motivated soldiers even in the nineteenth century.

Money and private trade have vanished entirely: citizens carry credit cards, checked off at national distribution warehouses/sample stores stocked identically everywhere via pneumatic tube networks from central warehouses, eliminating retail markup, salesmanship, and dishonest inducement to buy. Credit is non-transferable, non-hoardable in any meaningful way, and lapses at death aside from funeral provision, though personal property may be freely bequeathed — accumulation of goods is self-limiting since possessions can't be resold for profit. Housing varies in size and rent according to personal taste, funded from the same equal income. Domestic drudgery has been abolished through public laundries, communal kitchens, and labor-saving design, since with no permanent servant class, everyone shares interest in eliminating needless toil; only physicians retain a personalized, chosen relationship with patients, still paid via the national credit system rather than fees.
