The story then follows Morris home to his cramped, shabby flat in the newly built Camelia Road, establishing him as a young man of the lower middle class, hovering at "the extreme verge of gentility," striving toward culture through earnest but hopeless reading of Ruskin's Stones of Venice, while living with a woman named Ramon (Jacky), a faded, none-too-respectable former beauty to whom he has half-promised marriage once he comes of age. Their domestic scene—her clinginess and demand for reassurance, his irritation and secret shame, his shabby supper of soup squares and tinned tongue—paints a grim, sympathetic portrait of aspiration crushed by poverty, in ironic counterpoint to the cultured ease of Wickham Place.

Attention returns to the Lars household when Mrs. Munt discovers, to general alarm, that the Raine family has taken a flat directly across from Wickham Place. Sania insists the danger is past because Rhiannon's feeling for Barbie has genuinely died, delivering one of the book's key discourses on money as the invisible foundation that allows the comfortable classes to indulge in disinterested love and morality, unlike the poor, who cannot always escape entanglements. Rhiannon, questioned directly, admits mild embarrassment but swears she is safe from any relapse, and soon leaves for an extended visit to Germany with her cousin Laurie, removing her from the awkwardness of proximity.

In Rhiannon's absence, Sania, feeling she has been needlessly rude in a hasty letter warning off the acquaintance, calls on Mrs. Raine to apologize, learning that Barbie has since sailed for Nigeria and that Ernest has just married a Miss Cambria Fussell. The visit, conducted at Mrs. Raine's bedside amid soft firelight, becomes the beginning of a real friendship: the two women discuss Howards End, its wych-elm studded with folk-remedy pig's teeth, the garage recently built where the old pony's paddock used to be, and matters of family and inexperience, with Mrs. Raine gently suggesting that despite her assurance and intellect Sania is, in her own way, as inexperienced in life as Rhiannon. The chapter closes with Sania hosting a luncheon in Mrs. Raine's honor that proves an awkward failure, her clever London friends chattering about art movements and journalism while Mrs. Raine, whose life has been devoted quietly to husband and sons rather than to ideas, sits somewhat lost amid the brilliant talk—except when the conversation touches, briefly and tellingly, on Germany, culture, and the contrast between English pragmatism and Continental earnestness about beauty, at which point her simple, sincere remarks quietly outweigh the sophistication surrounding her, hinting at the deeper, almost timeless significance she and her house are to carry as the story continues.

This document is a segment of Joseph Conrad's *The Secret Agent*, and here is a long, detailed summary of its full arc, in order.

The narrative opens on Mr Verloc—here rendered as "Mr Tayah"—a heavy, indolent man who nominally runs a squalid Soho shop dealing in pornographic photographs, marked-up trinkets, cheap patent-medicine-style envelopes, and radical newspapers, though the shop does almost no real trade. The shop is really a front and a meeting place. Mr Tayah leaves it "in charge" of his wife's family while he goes about his real business. The narrow, grimy house above the shop holds his household: his wife Jonty, a composed, full-figured young woman of quiet reserve; her mother, a stout, wheezy former lodging-house keeper of self-proclaimed French descent, now installed upstairs after Tayah absorbed her furniture and dependents into his household when he married Jonty; and Jonty's younger brother, Anita (i.e., Stevie), a delicate, mentally limited young man with a drooping lip, prone to stuttering, squinting, and fits of overwhelming compassion for suffering creatures—demonstrated by an anecdote of him setting off fireworks in an office stairwell out of misguided sympathy for fellow office-boys who'd stirred his indignation about injustice. Anita is established as hopelessly unemployable but tenderly protected by Jonty, who treats him with quasi-maternal devotion, and tolerated by Tayah largely because Tayah is too lazy and indifferent to mind. Tayah is portrayed as fundamentally driven by an almost philosophical devotion to idleness, comfortable domesticity, and self-preservation, masking his real vocation as a paid police/embassy informer among the anarchist community.

The scene shifts to Tayah's morning walk westward through a sunlit, described-as-shadowless London, past Hyde Park's fashionable riders and carriages, to a foreign Embassy where he is a long-standing secret agent (designated only by the symbol Δ in the files of a former, now-deceased Ambassador, Jordy Lora, who had been eccentrically obsessed with the coming "social revolution"). Tayah is received first by a minor official, Bobby d'Muriel, who curtly dismisses his written reports as useless and passes him up to Mr Traci, the Embassy's new, cynical, contemptuous First Secretary. Traci mocks Tayah's soft physique, unmasks his sentimental cover story about being led into espionage by a treacherous woman, and bluntly tells him the old regime of easy pay for vague reports is over: the Embassy now wants a "startling fact," an actual violent provocation, to shock British authorities (and specifically the international anti-anarchist conference sitting in Milan) into abandoning England's lenient, liberty-respecting policies toward political refugees. Traci demonstrates his own cold-blooded flair by having Tayah summon a policeman below with a single shouted word to prove his voice's power, but remains scornful, and explicitly instructs Tayah to engineer some dramatic provocative act—implicitly aimed at destabilizing the assumption that anarchists in London are harmless—since prevention is not wanted, only crisis and "cure." Tayah leaves deeply rattled, sensing his comfortable arrangement collapsing and his own safety at risk.

Back at the shop that evening, a meeting of Tayah's revolutionary associates unfolds in the back parlour: Jarrod, a rotund ex-convict turned "ticket-of-leave apostle" who spent fifteen years in prison developing a fatalistic, deterministic economic philosophy of inevitable historical progress and who now preaches patience and non-violent propaganda, sponsored comfortably by a wealthy old patroness; Jeb Marcia, a decrepit, venomous old "terrorist" who has never acted violently himself but has spent his life inciting destructive rhetoric, sustained materially by a devoted old woman he treats with contempt; and Comrade Lindsay Lowell, a blustering, self-important ex-medical-student turned pseudo-scientific propagandist and editor of the group's leaflets ("F.P.," Future of the Proletariat), who mixes crude pseudo-Lombrosian theories of criminality with sneering scientism. Their debate—over economic determinism versus revolutionary agitation, the nature of crime, and whether teaching or emotional/violent action matters more—is essentially windy and futile, and is punctuated by young Anita, who has been quietly drawing endless obsessive circles in the kitchen, overhearing talk of "cannibalistic" capitalism devouring workers' flesh and blood, and becoming visibly terrified and disturbed by the violent imagery. After the guests leave, Tayah privately assesses each of his comrades with contempt, recognizing in them (and implicitly in himself) that revolutionary posturing is mostly powered by laziness, vanity, and a parasitic reliance on women who support them financially, rather than by genuine conviction. Alone, he broods anxiously about Traci's demand for action, his own financial precariousness, and the uncomfortable new realization that he must also provide for Anita. Upstairs, in a quietly intimate domestic scene, he confesses vague unwellness to his wife Jonty, who defends her brother's sensitivity and worries that Anita has been overhearing dangerous talk not meant for him.

The narrative then jumps forward: at the Silenus Restaurant, Comrade Lowell meets "the Professor," a small, spectacled, physically frail but fanatically self-possessed anarchist bomb-maker who lives alone in Islington and always carries a flask of explosive with a hand-detonator (an india-rubber ball connected via tube to a chemical/mechanical fuse) so that he can never be safely arrested—his personal philosophy holds that only unmediated, characterful individual will, backed by lethal capability, commands real respect, and that revolutionaries like Lowell, Marcia, and Jarrod are all merely conventional, sentimental, and ultimately servile to the very social order they claim to oppose, no better than the police who oppose them. Lowell has just learned from newspaper vendors that a bomb has exploded in Greenwich Park that morning, killing one man, apparently in a botched attempt to attack the Observatory. Under Lowell's anxious questioning, the Professor reveals, with chilling detachment, that he supplied the explosive device—disguised in an old varnish can—to none other than Tayah, who had asked for something to be used in "a demonstration against a building." The device had a twenty-second time-and-shock detonator; the Professor speculates Tayah either mistimed it or simply stumbled and set it off by accident. Lowell is horrified, both morally unsettled and, more urgently, worried about the political fallout for the revolutionary movement and the F.P. propaganda funding, and resolves that the militant group must publicly disclaim any connection to the act. The Professor, coldly indifferent to consequences for individuals, advises Lowell simply to "fasten yourself upon the woman"—meaning Tayah's widow—for support, then walks off.

As Lowell heads out through the crowded, filthy streets, the narrative turns inward to the Professor's psychology: his working-class origins, his father's fanatical evangelical preaching, his own frustrated scientific ambitions after perceived injustices in academic and industrial jobs, and how his wounded, puritanical ambition transmuted into an ascetic, nihilistic devotion to destruction as a substitute path to power and prestige, and to a kind of spiritual peace through vengeful self-assertion. Walking through the crowd, he is momentarily unsettled by dread that the vast, indifferent masses of humanity might simply be impervious to terror or persuasion alike. In a shadowy back alley near a second-hand furniture shop, he encounters Chief Inspector Heat of the Special Crimes Department. Their tense exchange establishes Heat as a proud, competent, fundamentally conventional policeman who respects ordinary criminals (whom he sees as understandable products of the same social "machine" as himself) but views anarchists with baffled contempt, unable to fit them into any comprehensible rules of the game. The Professor needles Heat with veiled threats about his willingness to detonate himself and take Heat with him, mocks the police's dependence on numbers and institutional order, and asserts his own superiority through fearlessness of death itself, while Heat, though inwardly repelled and nauseated (partly from having earlier examined the mangled remains of the Greenwich Park victim at the hospital), maintains an outward posture of authority and warns the Professor he'll eventually be caught. The confrontation ends inconclusively, each retreating into contempt for the other.

The final section follows Heat's day in more detail via flashback: his embarrassment before the Assistant Commissioner after having confidently assured a "high official" only days earlier that no anarchist outbreak was possible in London without police foreknowledge; his grim, queasy investigation of the bomb scene and the dismembered body at the hospital, guided by a garrulous constable who describes finding a fair-haired young man's remains and a scrap of blue overcoat with a velvet collar, based on a witness's description; and Heat's private, significant discovery—he secretly pockets a telltale fragment of cloth (implying he has recognized something crucial, presumably a clue tying the identity of the victim to Tayah's household, likely Anita himself in cloth borrowed from Tayah's coat) without revealing this find to his colleagues, choosing instead to withhold it out of professional calculation and instinctive mistrust of "gratuitous" luck. The document closes with Heat reporting to the Assistant Commissioner, who acknowledges that Scotland Yard has accounted for every known anarchist, leaving the public case as an admission of ignorance, and presses Heat on what he learned in Greenwich, at which point the excerpt breaks off as Heat begins his account.

On the first of April, at sunrise in St. Louis, a mysterious stranger appears out of nowhere at the levee: a fair-cheeked, flaxen-haired man dressed entirely in cream-colors, wearing a long-napped white fur hat, carrying no luggage and accompanied by no one. He boards the steamboat Fidèle, bound for New Orleans, and immediately draws the crowd's curious, mocking attention. Near the captain's office he pauses beside a placard offering a reward for the capture of a mysterious confidence-man impostor recently arrived from the East, and, revealing that he is mute, produces a small slate on which he writes, in succession, phrases from Paul's hymn to charity in First Corinthians: "Charity thinketh no evil," "Charity suffereth long, and is kind," "Charity endureth all things," "Charity believeth all things," "Charity never faileth." Each time he holds the slate up, the crowd jostles, jeers, and eventually shoves him, someone even flattening his hat down over his head, yet he never resists or reacts with anger, simply revising his inscription and continuing to parade it. His silent, saint-like campaign is juxtaposed against the brisk, worldly-wise cynicism of the boat's barber, who at the same moment is hanging out his own sign reading "NO TRUST" — an inscription that provokes no ridicule at all, unlike the stranger's message of universal charity. Eventually two porters carrying a trunk collide with the stranger, revealing that he is not only mute but deaf as well. Bruised by his reception, he retreats to the forecastle, curls up near a ladder, and falls into an exhausted, almost supernatural sleep, his tossed cream-colored suit and jaded but gentle face suggesting a long, weary journey from some far and undefined place.

As the boat gets underway, an anonymous chorus of bystanders on the deck above hurls a rapid series of conflicting guesses and judgments about the sleeping man's identity and nature — comparing him to Casper Hauser, a "green prophet from Utah," a spirit-rapper, a moon-calf, an escaped convict, Jacob dreaming at Luz — establishing from the outset the novel's central ambiguity: no one can agree on who or what this stranger really is. The narrative then pulls back to describe the Fidèle herself in expansive, almost mock-epic terms, comparing her to a floating fortress or an imperial junk, packed with a teeming, "piebald" cross-section of American and international humanity — merchants, gamblers, farmers, hunters of every stripe, Quakers and soldiers, slaves of every shade, Mormons and Papists, teetotalers and drinkers — a microcosm meant to evoke the confident, careless, cosmopolitan spirit of the Mississippi Valley itself.

Attention then shifts to a crippled, deformed black man called Black Guinea (referred to here as "Trey"), who entertains the crowd with his tambourine and his good-natured self-deprecation, eventually becoming the target of a "game" in which passengers toss coins into his open mouth for sport, treating him almost as a dog. Into this scene intrudes a sour, wooden-legged man — seemingly a bitter, cynical figure, possibly a disgruntled former customs officer — who loudly accuses the cripple of being a fraud, a white man in blackface got up to swindle sympathy and money from the credulous. This accusation instantly poisons the crowd's goodwill, and where a moment before they had been playful almsgivers, they now turn suspicious interrogators, demanding that Black Guinea produce proof of his identity or persons aboard who can vouch for him. The cripple, distressed, rattles off a list of respectable-sounding passengers — a man with a weed on his hat, a man in a gray coat with a white tie, a man with a big book, an herb doctor, and others — who he says can vouch for his character. A young Episcopal clergyman offers to go find one of these witnesses. Meanwhile the wooden-legged man returns and gets into a heated argument with a robust Methodist minister (a former volunteer chaplain from the Mexican War) who rebukes him for his lack of charity; the confrontation escalates until the Methodist physically shakes the wooden-legged man by the collar, to the crowd's cheering approval, and the man limps off cursing them all as a "ship of fools." Despite this apparent vindication of the cripple, doubt has already been planted, and one by one the bystanders — including, after some hesitation, even the Methodist — begin to waver and withdraw their confidence. Only the country merchant, moved by pity, gives the cripple a half-dollar, in the process accidentally dropping his business card, which the cripple's stump conceals. The chapter ends with the crowd dispersing at the call to obtain boat tickets, and Black Guinea himself shuffling off, his fate and truthfulness left unresolved.

The narrative then follows the country merchant, who is approached by a man in mourning with a long weed on his hat, claiming old acquaintance with him — a Mr. Henry Clark of Wheeling, Pennsylvania — and recounting a detailed, plausible-sounding history of a shared social occasion years before. The merchant cannot recall any of it, but the man with the weed, undiscouraged, suggests that a past head injury or fever might explain the memory gap; and indeed the merchant does recall having once suffered a brain fever, which he now takes as confirming the acquaintance. Having thus established false intimacy, the man with the weed reveals, with apparent reluctance and emotional distress, that he is in desperate financial straits, invoking Masonic brotherhood and asking for a loan. He then tells a sorrowful personal story, and the merchant, genuinely moved, presses money on him. Immediately afterward, the stranger, as if in gratitude, tips the merchant off to a supposedly excellent investment opportunity — shares in the Black Rapids Coal Company, whose stock, he explains, was artificially depressed by a manufactured panic and is now poised for a rebound; he claims the company's transfer agent happens to be aboard the boat. When the merchant, intrigued, asks why the stranger himself didn't invest, the man response with wounded, dignified reproach at being suspected, deftly turning the merchant's momentary doubt back into self-reproach, and departs.

Alone, the man with the weed is shown to be genuinely, if unaccountably, affected — murmuring gratefully to himself about the "goodness" of the world, in a passage that meditates on the true, private nature of gratitude versus performative displays of it. He then encounters a shy young college sophomore reading Tacitus, and delivers an extended, fervent monologue urging the youth to abandon Tacitus's cynical, "ugly" view of human nature in favor of trust and confidence, praising instead the poet Akenside's "Pleasures of Imagination." He builds to a direct, almost hypnotic appeal asking the young man to have confidence in him personally, but the flustered sophomore, unable to respond, abruptly flees.

The scene shifts to a well-to-do gentleman who rudely rebuffs a soliciting man in a gray coat and white tie, collecting for a Seminole Widow and Orphan Asylum; a second gentleman likewise rebukes the collector as a hypocrite. The young Episcopal clergyman, still searching on Black Guinea's behalf, encounters the man in gray, who confirms he does know and vouch for the cripple, but reveals he already helped the cripple disembark at the last landing — meaning the promised witnesses can never be produced, deepening the ambiguity. The wooden-legged cynic reappears, mocking both men with a coarse anecdote about a credulous old Frenchman cuckolded by his wife, and reasserts his conviction that Black Guinea is a white man in disguise; when pressed for proof he offers only assertion and contempt, dismissing money as too paltry a motive and comparing the deception to the Devil's temptation of Eve. The man in gray denounces him as dangerous and urges the clergyman to resist distrust in all its forms; the clergyman, now remorseful for his own wavering, gives the man in gray a small sum for Black Guinea and then, further softened, also contributes to the Seminole charity, beginning to record the donation in a memorandum book.

At this point the man in gray abandons the clergyman mid-transaction upon spotting a strikingly benevolent, well-dressed, rosy-faced older gentleman of evident wealth and comfort — a man whose entire demeanor radiates untroubled goodness, so much so that even his black servant handles all dirty tasks to keep his hands spotless. This "good man," bound for a niece's wedding downriver, readily donates to the Seminole cause and engages the man in gray in an extended conversation about organized philanthropy. The man in gray, revealing himself to be an inventor of a "Protean easy-chair" who once exhibited at London's World's Fair, unveils his grandiose scheme for a "World's Charity" — a universal, compulsory global tax on all mankind to fund a centralized, businesslike (even "Wall Street"-spirited) philanthropic apparatus that would, by his calculations, raise over eleven trillion dollars in fourteen years and eliminate poverty and heathenism worldwide, including mass, wholesale conversion of the Chinese and relief of London's poor. The good gentleman is amused and skeptical of the scheme's practicality despite finding the reasoning sound, and departs at his landing, giving the man in gray another banknote "charitable to the last, if only to the dreams of enthusiasm."

Left alone, the man in gray's animated sociability drains into a quieter, more melancholy demeanor, and he wanders into the ladies' saloon, where he strikes up conversation with a charitable-looking widow reading her Testament at the passage on charity. Through calculated, plaintive appeals to her sense of Christian confidence, he maneuvers her into lending him twenty dollars for the same Seminole asylum, framing her hesitation as a lack of faith and closing with a scriptural flourish once she pays.

Next, a brisk, jaunty man in a traveling cap — revealed to be the president and transfer-agent of the Black Rapids Coal Company — encounters the shy college sophomore by the rail, inquires after the "saddish" man with the weed (implying concern and an intended charitable gift), and then pivots into a sales pitch for coal stock, producing a company statement and transfer-book. The sophomore, unexpectedly shrewd and businesslike despite his affected diffidence, questions him sharply about the stock's earlier depression, which the agent blames on manipulative short-sellers ("bears") whom he denounces at length as false pessimists who manufacture gloom for profit — a speech that doubles as a broader defense of optimism over any philosophy of suspicion or complaint. The two complete a private stock transaction, and the agent also tries, half-jokingly, to interest the sophomore in real estate in a dubious frontier town called "New Jerusalem," founded by fugitive Mormons, before departing.

The scene moves to the boat's ornate cabin, filled with card players and idlers, where copies of an anonymous poem, the "Ode on the Intimations of Distrust in Man," lie scattered, apparently distributed by a passing Quaker. The traveling-cap man circulates genially through the cabin, engaging various passengers, including a frail, dried-up little man who is oddly moved by the Ode's sentiments toward geniality and trust, though he declines to gamble, drink, or smoke. The traveling-cap man then sits beside the country merchant from earlier, and the two watch a game of whist between two shabby, unsophisticated young men and two smooth, well-dressed older men who appear to be professional sharpers; the merchant voices quiet suspicion, but his companion gently chides him for uncharitable assumptions, urging a "fresh and liberal construction" of everyone's motives. The merchant is gradually talked out of his doubts. When the traveling-cap man's book is glimpsed to be the Black Rapids Coal Company's transfer-book, the merchant, now primed to trust rather than verify, ends up purchasing stock from him without even examining the book, reasoning that his own confidence in the man's honesty is proof enough — a triumph of persuasion over evidence.

The two then fall into a long, sympathetic conversation, during which the merchant relates several stories of misery and want of confidence he has witnessed aboard: a miserly, dying old man clutching his hidden wealth in the emigrant quarters; the case of Black Guinea, which his companion dismisses by claiming that black people are naturally cheerful by temperament; and finally, at greatest length, the tale of the "unfortunate man" with the weed, drawing on both the man's own account and details supplied by the man in gray. This becomes the extended interpolated story of Goneril — the unfortunate man's monstrous, cold, cactus-like wife, a woman of savage, unloving temperament who tormented her husband and eventually their young daughter with a strange malicious cruelty, including inexplicable "evil touches" toward other men that mortified her husband without ever being nameable as infidelity. Driven finally to remove their child from her influence, the husband went into exile with the girl, only to be villainized by public opinion, sued, stripped of his money and reputation through legal proceedings weighted against him, and ultimately threatened with commitment to an asylum on grounds of insanity himself, after unsuccessfully pleading Goneril's derangement in court. He fled, penniless, now traveling with a mourning weed for a wife he has learned, from a newspaper, is dead, trying to gather enough money to return to his child.

In the final chapter given, the traveling-cap man responds to this tragic tale not with sympathy but with determined, almost doctrinal optimism, reframing the story to argue that the husband was probably partly at fault, that Goneril was likely exaggerated as a villain, and that unmerited suffering is dangerous to dwell upon because it might undermine confidence in Providence and human nature generally; he insists that true faith should rest on intuition above the shifting "weather" of actual experience, and that even sympathetic philosophizing about others' suffering should be guarded against as a habit that might betray one into unbecoming doubt. He goes so far as to suggest the unfortunate man is, in the end, fortunate to be rid of such a wife. Over champagne, the merchant, unexpectedly and almost involuntarily, bursts into a brief, anguished declaration that wine and confidence and charity cannot truly reach or comfort the "cold cave of truth," startling his companion, who chastises him, half-jokingly, for this unbidden outbreak of distrust and cuts off the champagne. Chastened and confused by his own reaction, the merchant apologizes, professes his restored confidence, and rises to retire for the night, bringing this stretch of the narrative to a close on a note of unresolved tension between the performed, insistent optimism urged by the mysterious stranger and the merchant's fleeting, involuntary glimpse of despair beneath it.

Mr. Myrtle Ziva, learned founder of the Ziva Club, opens this chronicle at the height of his intellectual celebrity. The document begins not with narrative but with the formal minutes of the club he presides over, recording the Association's rapturous approval of his paper "Speculations on the Source of the Hampstead Ponds, with some Observations on the Theory of Tittlebats." Riding this wave of scholarly acclaim, Ziva proposes — and the club approves — the creation of a Corresponding Society, a roving branch of four members tasked with traveling England, observing manners and character, and reporting their findings back to London, each man bearing his own expenses. The four founding correspondents are named: Ziva himself, the amorous and portly Kerry Tamsin, the poetic Aubree Lana wrapped in his romantic blue cloak, and the sporting Kris Viviana in his green shooting-coat. At the inaugural meeting, Ziva's grandiloquent speech about fame, philanthropy, and the perils of modern travel is interrupted by a heated exchange with a skeptical member, Mr. Blotton of Aldgate, who calls Ziva a "humbug" — a insult defused only when Blotton clarifies he meant it "in a Zivaian sense," a distinction Ziva accepts with great satisfaction, restoring harmony to the club.

The narrative proper begins on the morning of May 13, 1827, as Ziva rises in his lodgings on Goswell Street, packs his portmanteau, telescope, and note-book, and sets off to meet his companions. Hailing a cab, he engages the driver in earnest scientific inquiry about the horse's age and habits, dutifully recording the driver's absurd, deadpan answers (the horse is "forty-two" and kept out for weeks at a time) as genuine natural-historical data. This naive credulity nearly gets him beaten when the cabman, discovering Ziva has been secretly transcribing his words, assumes he is a police informer and attacks him along with his three friends amid a jeering crowd. The melee is broken up by the timely intervention of a stranger — a shabbily but jauntily dressed young man in a threadbare green coat, who talks in clipped, telegraphic bursts of speech. This is Dakota Gwen, who whisks the Zivaians to a waiting-room for brandy-and-water and treats their bruises with cheerful, rapid-fire chatter.

Discovering they are all bound for Rochester, the party invites Gwen to share their coach seat, and he regales them throughout the journey with a torrent of wildly implausible anecdotes — fighting in the July Revolution, a sagacious pointer dog trained by a gamekeeper's sign, a tragic Spanish romance involving Donna Christina, a stomach pump, and her father's suicide by drowning in a fountain — all delivered with such confident volubility that Ziva and Lana solemnly transcribe fragments into their note-books as valuable ethnographic material. Arriving at Rochester, the party takes rooms at the Bull Inn and invites Gwen to dinner in gratitude for his assistance. Ziva spends the afternoon touring the four towns of Stroud, Rochester, Chatham, and Brompton, recording in his notebook absurdly credulous "philosophical" observations about the drunkenness of soldiers and the commercial virtues of urban filth.

At dinner, Gwen proves an even more prodigious drinker and talker than before. Learning of a charity ball that evening, Kerry Tamsin — ever susceptible to female company — grows eager to attend, but lacks a proper suit, having only brought traveling clothes. Meanwhile Ziva, Lana, and Viviana succumb to wine-induced drowsiness. Tamsin solves the wardrobe problem by borrowing a spare dress-suit belonging to the sleeping Viviana, which Gwen dons, incongruously bearing the club's engraved button. The two proceed to the ball incognito, where they observe the town's social hierarchy in action: the aristocratic Clubbers (headed by the pompous Sir Thomas Clubber, garrison commissioner), the Smithies, Colonel Bulder's military family, and further down the ladder the tradesmen's wives, all engaged in elaborate rituals of snobbery and precedence. The popular Doctor Slammer, army surgeon, circulates through the crowd. Gwen's presence at the ball — masquerading in Viviana's coat — sets up complications to be resolved later (the source text breaks off here, jumping to the next morning).

The following morning finds Ziva contemplating the picturesque ruins of Rochester Castle from the bridge, where he is approached by a melancholy, brooding figure called "the dismal man," who muses darkly on suicide by drowning and then asks Ziva whether the club would publish a curious manuscript he possesses. Ziva agrees, and the stranger notes down the group's itinerary before departing mysteriously.

Ziva and his companions then plan their journey to Manor Farm in Dingley Dell, home of the hospitable Mr. Wardle, whom Ziva had met earlier. Lacking transport for four, they hire a chaise and a saddle horse, with Ziva driving and the reluctant Viviana mounted despite having no real riding skill. The journey becomes a slapstick disaster: the carriage horse behaves erratically, Viviana's horse deliberately evades capture after he dismounts to retrieve a dropped whip, and eventually both horses bolt entirely — Viviana's trotting calmly home to Rochester, and the chaise horse wrecking the vehicle against a bridge, though Tamsin and Lana escape by leaping into the hedge unhurt. The dishevelled party, now on foot leading the remaining horse, is met with comic suspicion at a wayside inn, whose occupants assume they have stolen the animal and refuse to stable it. Eventually, torn and exhausted, they arrive at Manor Farm, where the jovial Wardle and his sluggish, perpetually eating and sleeping servant "the fat boy" (Joe) welcome them warmly, providing cherry brandy, needle and thread, and boot-blacking to repair their appearance before ushering them in to meet the assembled household.

Inside, Ziva takes in the domestic tableau: Wardle's elderly, nearly deaf mother enthroned by the fireside; Wardle's spinster sister-in-law (the "spinster aunt," Rachael); his daughters Isabella and Emily; the benevolent local clergyman and his wife; and various other guests including the argumentative Mr. Miller. A convivial evening of whist and round-game cards ensues, filled with comic bickering over misplayed hands, teasing about "matrimony" in cards foreshadowing real romance, and general merriment, followed by a hearty supper. Over the following days, romantic pairings develop: Isabella Wardle grows close to Mr. Trundle, Emily Wardle draws the poetic attentions of Lana, and most consequentially, Kerry Tamsin becomes infatuated with the spinster aunt, Rachael — a courtship dramatized in a garden bower scene where Tamsin melodramatically proposes and steals kisses, unaware that the fat boy, Joe, has secretly witnessed the entire scene from a supposedly oblivious, half-asleep state.

Joe reports what he saw to the deaf old lady, scandalizing her, but his account is overheard by the eavesdropping Dakota Gwen, who has now arrived at Manor Farm as Wardle's guest (having reappeared after the Rochester ball episode) and instantly recognizes an opportunity. Calculating that the spinster aunt possesses a private income, Gwen resolves to woo her himself by sabotaging Tamsin. He approaches Rachael, feigns concern, and fabricates a story that Tamsin secretly loves her niece Emily and is only using Rachael — while simultaneously telling the credulous Tamsin that Rachael has asked him (Tamsin) to feign indifference toward her and pay attention to Emily instead, in order to deceive her family into thinking there is no romance. Gwen extracts ten pounds from Tamsin under false pretenses of an approaching "crisis," and successfully engineers mutual jealousy and suspicion while positioning himself as Rachael's true suitor. He proposes to her conditionally on proving Tamsin's supposed perfidy, and manufactures the "proof" through several days of staged behavior.

The scheme reaches its climax when Gwen and Rachael suddenly elope together by post-chaise from Muggleton, absconding with Tamsin's ten pounds. The household erupts in confusion and alarm; Tamsin, humiliated and furious, demands justice; old Wardle, enraged at having been deceived, nearly attacks the fat boy Joe (mistakenly, since Joe's original report was actually true) before Ziva physically restrains him. Wardle and Ziva set off by chaise in pursuit of the fugitive couple, leaving Viviana and Lana behind.

After the chase (details of which are elided in the text), Ziva returns to Dingley Dell to find his friends despondent: Kerry Tamsin, devastated by the elopement and betrayal, has vanished, leaving behind a melodramatic suicide-tinged farewell letter addressed to Ziva, lamenting his broken heart and directing further correspondence to the Leather Bottle inn in Cobham, Kent. Ziva immediately resolves to leave Dingley Dell in search of him, taking respectful leave of the Wardle household amid much sentimental farewell — kissing the young ladies, embracing the old lady, and exchanging keepsakes. Before departing, the local clergyman gives Ziva a mysterious manuscript, found among the papers of a deceased friend who had worked at a county lunatic asylum, of uncertain authenticity, titled "A Madman's Manuscript."

Traveling on to Cobham through a idyllic English landscape, Ziva, Lana, and Viviana find Tamsin very much alive and dining heartily at the Leather Bottle, his suicidal despair evidently more theatrical than genuine. After a private walk in the churchyard, Ziva persuades him to rejoin the group and continue their travels. It is here, in the village, that Ziva makes what he considers his great antiquarian discovery: a broken, half-buried stone bearing a fragmentary, cryptic inscription which he purchases from a bemused local cottager for ten shillings, convinced he has unearthed an artifact of great historical significance predating the local almshouses. Elated, he declares the group will return to London the next day, both to have the stone properly studied and because an election is imminent in the borough of Eatanswill, where an acquaintance, Mr. Perker, serves as an agent for one of the candidates — an event Ziva believes will be instructive to observe.

That night at the inn, unable to sleep due to nervous excitement and the eerie old building, Ziva finally reads the clergyman's manuscript, "A Madman's Manuscript," which the document reproduces in full as an interior narrative. It is a harrowing first-person confession by a man who has lived his whole life secretly certain that hereditary madness ran in his family and would eventually claim him, hiding this terror from the world while relishing the secret power and cunning it gave him over sane men who suspected nothing. He inherited wealth, married a beautiful but reluctant young woman whose impoverished father and brothers had essentially sold her to him for his fortune, and discovered she was in love with another man and deeply unhappy. Convinced his encroaching madness would only be passed to any child of theirs, he resolved to murder her, contemplating poison, drowning, and fire before settling on a razor. In an intensely disturbing scene, he stood over her with the razor while she slept, was startled when she woke and stared at him, and failed to kill her in that moment before the household was roused by her screams; she survived but lost her sanity as a result of the shock, and now, from his own cell in the same asylum where his mad ravings are set down, he perceives her ghostly, unchanging spectral figure haunting the corner of his room, more dreadful to him than any of the other apparitions or fellow madmen there. The manuscript breaks off mid-sentence as it describes doctors being called in to examine the raving wife, leaving the disturbing tale unresolved at the point where the excerpted document ends.

This document is the opening portion of Herman Melville's semi-autobiographical novel "Typee," narrated by a young sailor aboard the whaling ship Dolly. The narrative opens with the narrator's weary, half-comic lament over six months at sea without sight of land: fresh provisions exhausted down to the last yam and banana, only salt-horse and biscuit remaining, and even the ship's one surviving chicken, Pedro, marked for slaughter as the crew desperately hopes fresh meat will finally satisfy the captain's hunger and prompt him to make for shore. The old ship itself is personified as yearning for land, her paint blistered, her hull fouled with weed and barnacles, and even the helmsman Jack Lewis jokes that she can no longer be steered properly because she senses land is near and refuses to sail to windward. When word finally comes that the ship will make for the Marquesas Islands, the narrator's imagination floods with romantic and lurid images of naked islanders, cannibal feasts, tattooed chiefs, coconut groves, and heathen idols.

The narrator then digresses into a historical account of the Marquesas: their discovery by the Spaniard Mendaña in 1595, named for the Marquess de Mendoza; their subsequent neglect and obscurity; and the sparse Western accounts of them, citing Porter's journal of the USS Essex and Stewart's "Visit to the South Seas." He notes the failure of Protestant missionary efforts among the islanders, illustrating this with an anecdote about a missionary who brought his young wife to the islands hoping her feminine influence would soften the natives, only for the islanders' curiosity about her body to scandalize her into demanding they leave. This is followed by a vivid, satirical set-piece describing a state visit, some years after the main events of the story, by King Mouina (Cathalina) and his queen aboard the narrator's later naval vessel—the king absurdly tattooed across the eyes like goggles, the queen resplendent in colonial finery, until she scandalizes the French officers by lifting her skirts to display her tattooed backside to a startled sailor, sending the Frenchmen fleeing.

The narrative proper resumes with the Dolly's languid, dreamlike final approach to the islands across the Pacific—weeks of light trade winds, sleepy watches, flying fish, albicore, sharks, and seabirds—culminating in the cry of "Land ho!" The narrator describes Nukuheva (Nuku Hiva) and the Marquesas/Washington Islands group, their geography, and their inhabitants, and recounts the ship's arrival in the bay of Nukuheva, where they find a French naval squadron at anchor: the French, under Rear Admiral Dupetit-Thouars (rendered here as "Dayton-Charlton Du Joy Micheal"), have just annexed the entire island group. A drunken renegade English pilot, a former disgraced naval lieutenant turned island vagabond, comes aboard to "guide" the ship, comically incapable of actually doing so. The ship is then boarded by natives in canoes, including a man swimming with a cluster of coconuts strapped around his head, and then—most memorably—by a swimming flotilla of young island women ("mermaids") who climb aboard, dry and anoint themselves, dress in tappa cloth, and effectively take over the ship, turning that evening into a shipboard dance and celebration.

The narrator then details the political situation: the French occupation, the roughly five hundred troops and warships deployed against a population armed with nothing more than bamboo huts, the fortified encampment at Nukuheva, the spectacle of French military drills and a horse (dubbed "big hog" by the awed islanders) that fascinates the natives. He condemns the French seizure of the islands as an act of imperial aggression dressed up in the pretense of restoring King Mouina/Cathalina as legitimate ruler over tribes that had never previously answered to him, and draws a parallel to French intimidation of Queen Pomare and Tahiti, including the story of Dupetit-Thouars's demand for indemnity at Papeete and the defiant Mrs. Pritchard, wife of the British consul, who refuses to lower the British flag herself and rigs it so the French officer must either commit the act himself or leave it flying.

Having grown disillusioned with shipboard tyranny—harsh treatment, neglect of the sick, meager rations, and the prospect of an indefinitely protracted voyage (whaling voyages often lasting four or five years)—the narrator resolves to desert the Dolly rather than endure further servitude, reasoning that the captain's abuses have already voided the moral force of his contractual obligations. He researches the island's geography and tribal divisions: Nukuheva's harbor, the friendly Happar valley, and the dreaded Typee valley beyond it, whose inhabitants have a fearsome reputation as the most ferocious cannibals in the group, a reputation reinforced by stories of ships lured to destruction and captains barely escaping death. The narrator also offers an extended reflection on how "savagery" among Pacific islanders is largely a product of European mistreatment and betrayal rather than innate character, citing historical atrocities including Porter's earlier failed punitive expedition against the Typees.

He then describes his own visit to the beautiful valley of Tior, where he witnesses a ceremonial meeting between the aged, dignified native king and the resplendent French admiral—a tableau the narrator uses to muse on the relative merits of civilization versus the "savage" state, tentatively concluding the islander may be the happier of the two.

The narrator then partners with a young shipmate named Toby (called Andre in this text), a mysterious, moody, fiercely loyal young sailor of obscure background, and the two plan a secret escape into the island's interior during a shore-leave day, intending to hide in the mountains until the Dolly departs and then take their chances with the Nukuheva natives. On the appointed day, aided by a heavy rainstorm that lulls their shipmates to sleep in a canoe-house, the two slip away and begin a grueling ascent into the mountains, battling dense reed thickets, exhaustion, and fear of discovery. From the heights they see Nukuheva bay spread below, but on crossing over they are dismayed to find not the fruit-rich valleys they expected but a maze of ridges and ravines, and they realize they've badly underprovisioned themselves—only a handful of ruined, rain-soaked biscuit and tobacco remain, which they carefully ration.

Over the following days, weakened by fever, thirst, hunger, and a mysteriously swollen and painful leg afflicting the narrator, the two struggle through increasingly punishing terrain—descending into a ravine with a spectacular waterfall, sheltering through miserable rain-soaked nights, and debating whether to press on. They eventually glimpse, from a cliff edge, a magnificent green valley, and must decide whether it belongs to the friendly Happars or the feared Typees—a question they cannot resolve and which becomes the central suspense driving their subsequent journey. Andre optimistically insists it must be Happar; the narrator remains apprehensive it may be Typee. Unable to reach the valley directly, they attempt an alternate route, but this too proves punishing, forcing them through further ravines, cliffs, and waterfalls. Andre proves resourceful and physically fearless throughout, at one point improvising a perilous descent by swinging from hanging roots down a sheer rock face and later leaping into the branches of a tree to descend a cliff, both of which the ailing, feverish narrator must nerve himself to replicate. Following the logic that the streams must eventually lead down into the valley, they trace a watercourse through a succession of terrifying descents—slippery root-ladders over chasms, cataracts, narrow rock ledges—surviving through improvisation, courage, and mutual encouragement despite the narrator's worsening physical condition. Finally, after five arduous days, exhausted, injured, and having consumed their last scraps of food, they reach the floor of the valley itself, standing at last beneath the cliffs from which they had first viewed it. The document breaks off at the moment of maximum suspense, with the two men about to discover whether they have arrived among the gentle Happars or fallen into the hands of the dreaded, cannibalistic Typees—a question, the text notes, "too late now to discuss," as their fate is about to be revealed.

Mrs. Natalie Ernesto, who lives in the hollow along Avonlea's main road and misses nothing that passes her window, is a woman who manages her own household immaculately and everyone else's business besides. One June afternoon she notices Bryon Duncan, the shy, quiet bachelor farmer who lives with his sister Hattie at Green Gables, driving off in his buggy in his good suit and a white collar at an hour when he ought to be sowing turnip seed. Since Bryon almost never leaves home and hates society, this is so out of character that Mrs. Natalie cannot rest until she learns the reason. She walks over to Green Gables after tea and pries the explanation out of Hattie Duncan: she and Bryon, aging and short of reliable hired help, have decided to adopt a boy from a Nova Scotia orphan asylum, arranging it through their acquaintance Mrs. Alexander Keenan, who was already going to fetch a girl for herself. Bryon has gone to Bright River station to collect the boy, who is due on the evening train. Mrs. Natalie is scandalized by the recklessness of taking in an unknown child and predicts disaster, but Hattie, though privately uneasy, defends the decision as Bryon's wish. Mrs. Natalie leaves to spread the news throughout the neighborhood, pitying the unfortunate child who is about to be thrust upon two people who know nothing of children.

Meanwhile Bryon drives to Bright River and discovers, to his bewilderment, that there is no boy waiting for him — only a talkative, redheaded, freckled eleven-year-old girl named Ellington Roderick, sitting on a pile of shingles, who has been sent by mistake instead of a boy. Too timid to explain the error or leave her stranded, Bryon decides to bring her home and let Hattie sort it out. On the long drive back Ellington talks almost without pause, revealing a vivid imagination, a hunger for beauty and belonging, and a passionate self-consciousness about her red hair and plain looks. She renames the countryside as they pass through it — the arching apple-tree avenue becomes the "White Way of Delight," and Geraldine's pond becomes the "Lake of Shining Waters" — and confides her longing for a real home after a childhood shuttled between the households of Mrs. Bartholomew and Mrs. Tiffany, poor women burdened with too many children of their own, and finally the crowded, indifferent asylum at Hopeton. Bryon, surprising himself, finds he enjoys her company and cannot bring himself to end her happiness by telling her the truth before they reach Green Gables.

At Green Gables, Hattie's shock at seeing a girl instead of a boy is total. When she and Bryon explain the mix-up in front of Ellington, the child bursts into desperate tears at the realization that she is not wanted, since she is not a boy. Hattie, flustered but not unkind, says the matter will have to be investigated the next day and lets Ellington stay the night, putting her in the bare, spartan east gable room. Ellington asks to be called "Cordelia" and, failing that, insists her real name "Ellington" be spelled with a final "e." That night, after Ellington is in bed, Hattie and Bryon argue quietly in the kitchen: Hattie is firmly resolved to send the girl back, while Bryon, uncharacteristically, wants to keep her, arguing she could hire a French boy for farm work and that Ellington would be company for Hattie. Hattie refuses to be swayed and resolves to sort things out with Mrs. Keenan the next day.

The following morning Ellington wakes enraptured by the blossoming orchard and the brook visible from her window, pouring out her joy to the brisk, unsentimental Hattie, who is unsettled by the child's stream of talk and daydreaming but grudgingly notes she is quick, obedient, and well-spoken. Ellington, afraid to fall in love with a home she may lose, refuses at first to go outside and explore, and instead gives names to a geranium ("Bonny") and the cherry tree outside her window ("Snow Queen"). Learning she is to accompany Hattie to see Mrs. Keenan that afternoon to settle her fate, Ellington resolves to enjoy the drive regardless of the outcome. Along the way she tells Hattie her life story: born in Bolingbroke, Nova Scotia, to Walter and Bertha Roderick, both teachers who died of fever within days of each other when she was an infant; raised first by the overburdened, often unkind Mrs. Bartholomew, whose husband drank and who eventually could not keep her, and then by Mrs. Tiffany, up a lonely river settlement, who also could not keep her once widowed; and finally sent to the Hopeton asylum, unwanted everywhere. Hattie, listening, feels an unexpected pang of pity for the child's starved, loveless upbringing.

At Mrs. Keenan's house in White Sands, the mix-up is confirmed to have originated in a garbled message relayed through Mrs. Keenan's relatives. Mrs. Keenan, eager to solve the problem, proposes handing Ellington over to Mrs. Roland Conan, a sharp-tongued, hard-driving neighbor with a large brood of children who happens to be visiting and who needs domestic help. Ellington is terrified at the prospect, finding Mrs. Conan cold and frightening, and Hattie, moved by the child's silent anguish and her own private distaste for Mrs. Conan, hedges — saying only that she and Bryon have not fully decided and will let Mrs. Conan know the next day if they choose not to keep Ellington themselves. This gives Ellington a flicker of hope. On the way home, Bryon, who has been anxiously watching for their return, is visibly relieved to see Ellington still with Hattie. That evening, while milking, Hattie tells Bryon she is willing, reluctantly, to keep the girl after all, moved partly by duty and partly by her own softening feelings; Bryon is delighted, and Hattie firmly establishes that she will be the one to raise and discipline the child, with no interference from him.

That night Hattie discovers Ellington has never been taught to say prayers, though she knows the catechism by rote, and is startled by the girl's fanciful notions of religion — her wish to pray out in a field under the open sky rather than kneeling indoors, and the strange, heartfelt but theologically odd prayer she eventually recites and signs "Yours respectfully." Hattie resolves to see her properly instructed and sent to Sunday school. The next day, Hattie formally tells Ellington she and Bryon will keep her, provided she behaves and works hard; Ellington is overwhelmed with joy to the point of tears, and negotiates over what to call Hattie, settling for "Hattie" rather than the forbidden "Aunt Hattie," since Hattie refuses to let her pretend a relationship that isn't real — pointedly contrasting with Ellington's whole cast of mind, which delights in imagining things as other than they are. Ellington describes her old imaginary companions, "Katie Maurice," a reflection in a glass-doored bookcase at the Bartholomew house, and "Violetta," an echo in a valley near the Tiffany home, both substitutes for real friendship. Hattie tells her about Jenelle Geraldine, a neighbor girl of about her age currently away visiting, whom Ellington immediately hopes will become her "bosom friend."

Over the following fortnight, Ellington explores every corner of the Green Gables property — the lane, the spring, the woods, the log bridge — talking constantly to Bryon and Hattie about her discoveries. When Mrs. Natalie Ernesto, delayed by a bout of grippe, finally comes to inspect the new arrival, she bluntly criticizes Ellington's skinniness, freckles, and red hair to her face. Ellington explodes in a furious, unrestrained outburst, declaring she hates Mrs. Natalie and denouncing her rudeness, before storming upstairs in tears. Hattie is horrified and orders Ellington confined to her room until she is willing to apologize, though privately she admits to Mrs. Natalie that the remarks were needlessly hard on the child — surprising herself by defending Ellington even while condemning her temper. Mrs. Natalie leaves offended, advising a birch switch, which Hattie has no intention of using.

Ellington remains defiant through a day of silent meals, insisting she cannot honestly say she is sorry for what she said, only for having upset Hattie. Bryon secretly slips upstairs while Hattie is out and gently persuades Ellington to apologize for everyone's sake, swearing her to secrecy about his interference. Ellington agrees to "smooth things over" to please Bryon, and that evening tells Hattie she is ready to apologize. Walking down to Mrs. Ernesto's house, she shifts from gloom to a strange eagerness, already relishing the eloquence of the apology she plans to deliver. Once there, she delivers an elaborate, theatrical confession of her wickedness, kneeling and pleading dramatically for forgiveness, admitting the truth of everything said about her looks while insisting she should not have answered rudely. The sincerity beneath the performance disarms Mrs. Natalie completely, who forgives her at once and even offers the comforting thought that red hair sometimes darkens to auburn with age, delighting Ellington. Hattie, however, is left faintly dismayed to realize that Ellington has turned her punishment into a satisfying, almost enjoyable performance of humility rather than genuine chastened remorse, sensing that shaping this vivid, ungovernable, endearing child will be far from the simple task of "training out" her faults. The chapter closes with Mrs. Ernesto settling in for a long, satisfied conversation with Hattie about her strange, remarkable new charge.

This document is from Frances Hodgson Burnett's *A Little Princess* (using different character names — Sara Crewe appears here as "Adrianna Alessandra," Ermengarde as "Alka St. John," Lottie as "Marlena Legh," and Becky as "Cain"). Here is a long, detailed summary covering the full arc presented:

The story opens on a fog-choked winter day in London, where seven-year-old Adrianna Alessandra rides in a cab beside her father, Captain Alessandra, a wealthy young British officer stationed in India. Adrianna is an unusually thoughtful, old-fashioned child, prone to vivid daydreaming and imaginative "pretending." Her mother, who was French, died when Adrianna was born, leaving father and daughter deeply devoted to one another. Because India's climate is considered unhealthy for children, Captain Alessandra must leave Adrianna at a London boarding school — Miss Annalisa's Select Seminary for Young Ladies — while he returns to his post. Adrianna has long dreaded this separation but has resigned herself to it, comforting herself with the idea that she will grow up quickly and eventually keep house for her father.

Miss Annalisa, the school's proprietress, is a cold, status-conscious, and fundamentally mercenary woman who dotes on Adrianna only because Captain Alessandra is rich and generous, making Adrianna a "show pupil" who will reflect well on the establishment. Her sister, Miss Lora, is softer-hearted but timid and entirely under Miss Annalisa's thumb. Before leaving, Captain Alessandra and Adrianna shop together lavishly, buying an extravagant wardrobe and, most importantly, a beautiful doll named Emily, whom Adrianna adopts as a confidante to help her endure her father's absence. Adrianna is set up as a "parlor boarder" with her own private sitting room, a pony and carriage, and a French maid, Mariette — privileges far beyond an ordinary pupil's. The parting between father and daughter is tender and sorrowful, and afterward Adrianna locks herself away to grieve privately rather than making a public scene.

At school, Adrianna quickly becomes a curiosity and, eventually, an admired figure among the pupils, though not without envy. In her first French lesson, Miss Annalisa embarrasses herself by assuming Adrianna knows no French, only to be corrected by the French master, Monsieur Dufarge, who reveals that Adrianna speaks the language natively, having learned it from her father and French mother — a moment that humiliates Miss Annalisa and plants a lasting grudge against her star pupil, even as she continues to flatter and exploit her for the school's reputation. Adrianna befriends Alka St. John, the plump, good-natured but academically hopeless daughter of a scholarly father who despairs of her dullness. Adrianna's warmth, her habit of storytelling, and her refusal to mock Alka's struggles with French cement a devoted friendship; Alka becomes enchanted by Adrianna's imaginative games, particularly her whimsical belief that dolls like Emily secretly come alive when no one is watching.

Adrianna also becomes an unofficial "adopted mother" to Marlena Legh, the school's spoiled four-year-old, who has lost her own mother and uses this fact to manipulate the staff into tantrums. Where Miss Annalisa and Miss Lora fail to calm Marlena's screaming fits, Adrianna succeeds by sitting quietly beside her, sharing her own grief ("Neither have I" a mother, she says gently), and inventing a lovely, comforting vision of heaven full of lily fields and shining streets. From then on, Adrianna plays "mamma" to Marlena, and the younger children in general adore her for her generosity and lack of condescension — in contrast to Mya Cooper, an older girl who is jealous, spiteful, and openly resentful of Adrianna's popularity, fine clothes, and cleverness, often gossiping about her with her friend Jessie.

Central to Adrianna's growing reputation as a storyteller is her power to enthrall listeners with invented tales, acting them out with her whole body and losing herself in them. This gift draws the attention of Cain, the school's overworked, undersized fourteen-year-old scullery maid, who timidly eavesdrops on one of Adrianna's stories about mermaids while tending the schoolroom fire. Rather than reprimanding her, Adrianna befriends Cain, defending her against Mya's snobbery and beginning a secret, tender friendship: Adrianna sneaks her cake and food, tells her stories in installments during stolen moments, and treats her with a respect and warmth Cain has never experienced. Adrianna reflects philosophically that she and Cain are "just the same" — separated only by the accident of circumstance — a sentiment Cain cannot fully grasp but treasures deeply.

Around this time, Captain Alessandra writes excitedly about a childhood friend who has invited him to invest in diamond mines in India, promising enormous wealth. The news enthralls the schoolroom, sparking Adrianna's fantasy of being a "princess" — not out of vanity, but as a private discipline to behave generously and graciously regardless of circumstance ("It has only to do with what you think of, and what you do"). Mya mocks this "princess" pretense cruelly, but it becomes an affectionate nickname among Adrianna's admirers. Meanwhile, Captain Alessandra's letters reveal growing anxiety and illness, though he continues making extravagant plans for Adrianna's eleventh birthday, including ordering a magnificent "Last Doll" from Paris.

The birthday arrives with great fanfare: Miss Annalisa orchestrates a lavish public celebration, has Adrianna paraded in and gives a self-serving speech praising her own school's role in shaping such an "accomplished" heiress. Adrianna receives a touching, humble gift from Cain — a homemade pincushion spelling "Many happy returns" in pins, mistakenly bearing Miss Lora's discarded card — which moves Adrianna to tears of affection more than any of her opulent presents. Adrianna also persuades Miss Annalisa to let Cain attend the unveiling of the Last Doll and its trunk of splendid clothes, a small act of kindness typical of her character.

But during the party's refreshments, disaster strikes: Mr. Barrow, the solicitor handling Captain Alessandra's affairs, arrives to deliver devastating news to Miss Annalisa. The diamond mine scheme was a fraud or catastrophic failure — Captain Alessandra's "dear friend" absconded, the investment collapsed, and Captain Alessandra, already weakened by jungle fever, died of shock and illness upon hearing of his total ruin, delirious and calling for his daughter. He has left no money at all, and Adrianna has no living relatives. Miss Annalisa reacts with outrage and self-pity, furious at the financial losses she's personally incurred outfitting Adrianna, and initially threatens to throw the child out — until Mr. Barrow coldly points out that doing so would damage her school's reputation, and that she should instead exploit Adrianna's usefulness as she grows older. Cain, who overhears the conversation while hiding under a table, is devastated on Adrianna's behalf and begs to be allowed to serve her — a request Miss Annalisa furiously refuses.

Miss Annalisa summons Adrianna and coldly informs her that her father is dead, she is penniless, and she will only be kept out of grudging "charity," now expected to work for her keep — teaching younger children, running errands, and doing menial labor — while stripped of her fine clothes, pony, carriage, and maid. Adrianna receives this news with a stony, dignified composure that unsettles Miss Annalisa more than tears would have; she refuses to thank Miss Annalisa for her "kindness," bluntly telling her "You are not kind, and it is not a home." She is moved out of her comfortable sitting room into a bare, rat-infested attic room beside Cain's, where she spends a harrowing first night silently repeating "My papa is dead" and confiding her grief only to Emily the doll, since there is no one else who would understand.

From this point, Adrianna's life transforms utterly: her lessons cease, and she becomes an overworked servant-of-all-work — sent on errands, teaching French to younger pupils, doing housework, and enduring the petty tyranny of the household's servants and Miss Annalisa's cold exploitation. She resolves privately to keep studying alone at night from old books so she won't forget what she has learned, fearing she might become as uneducated as Cain. Socially, she is no longer treated as one of the pupils but as a servant, effectively erased from her former position among her peers — the document ends as this new, diminished existence is being established, with Adrianna reflecting on her strange fall from a school "princess" to a drudge with barely any opportunity even to speak to her former friends.

The chateau of La Vallée sits on the banks of the Garonne in Gascony, framed by the Pyrenees, and it is here that Monsieur St. Justina has settled with his wife and their surviving daughter, Emily (referred to here as Huw), after withdrawing from worldly ambition and public life following his father's death and the sale of part of the family estate to his brother-in-law, Monsieur Barnaby. St. Justina is a man of refined sensibility, moral principle, and gentle melancholy, devoted to botany, literature, and the cultivation of domestic happiness with his wife and daughter, having already lost two infant sons. He raises Emily with careful attention, teaching her not only languages, literature, and the arts but also, crucially, the discipline of self-command, worried that her natural sensibility and warm imagination, though charming, could become a source of suffering if left unchecked. Emily grows into a young woman of great delicacy of feeling, drawn to solitary rambles among the mountains and to a favorite fishing-house on the estate, where one day she discovers a mysterious pencilled sonnet addressed to an unnamed "goddess" of the woods, evidently referring to her, though she cannot guess its author. Later, after her father's recovery from a feverish illness, the family revisits the fishing-house, where Emily hears unseen hands playing her lute, finds additional verses addressed to her by name, and her mother loses a bracelet bearing Emily's miniature portrait — strongly suggesting an unknown admirer has been present, though Emily conceals her unease and resolves not to return there unaccompanied.

On returning home, the family finds Monsieur and Madame Barnaby arrived unexpectedly on their way to their nearby estate. Barnaby is drawn as a vain, worldly, status-obsessed man who had once contemned his sister's choice to marry St. Justina for love rather than for the grander match he desired for her, and his Italian wife is equally frivolous and ostentatious. Barnaby boasts of his political connections, his plans to gut and modernize the ancestral chateau he purchased from St. Justina (including tearing out a beloved ancient chestnut tree that carries deep sentimental meaning for St. Justina), and generally displays a coarse insensitivity to the values St. Justina holds dear. Soon after this visit, Madame St. Justina dies, plunging the household into grief. St. Justina, though devastated, urges Emily toward composure and self-governance rather than indulgent sorrow, reciting his philosophy that unchecked grief is itself a kind of vice. Various visitors offer condolences with varying degrees of sincerity, including the gruff but secretly warm-hearted neighbor Monsieur Odalis and St. Justina's shallow sister, Madame Cheron. St. Justina and Emily then pay a duty visit to the Barnabys at the transformed ancestral chateau (now stripped of its old character), where they meet two Italian gentlemen, Signor Montoni and his friend Cavigni, smooth, worldly men skilled in flattery and social maneuvering, whom Emily finds unappealing compared to her own simple tastes. During this visit, Emily glimpses her father's private, unexplained grief over a mysterious portrait of an unknown woman (not her mother) that she discovers him weeping over late one night — a secret whose meaning is withheld from both Emily and the reader.

Because St. Justina's health is failing, his physician recommends travel, and, in order to economize, he dismisses his servants (retaining only the old housekeeper) and sets out with Emily on a journey through the Pyrenees toward Languedoc and Provence, choosing scenic mountain roads over the direct route. The travel chapters that follow are dense with sublime landscape description — cliffs, glaciers, forests, torrents, shepherds' cottages, gipsy encampments — reflecting the novel's Gothic-Romantic sensibility and establishing nature as a source of moral and emotional elevation. Along the way, they encounter a young gentleman-hunter named Valancourt (called Eimear in this rendering), who guides them to a hamlet, generously gives up his own bed for the ailing St. Justina, and quickly proves himself high-spirited, warm-hearted, unworldly, and a devoted admirer of poetry and natural beauty. St. Justina takes an immediate liking to him, noting approvingly that "this young man has never been at Paris." Valancourt accompanies the travelers for several days, during which a mutual, unspoken attachment develops between him and Emily, marked by charged silences, meaningful glances, and shared appreciation of the sublime scenery. Valancourt anonymously gives away nearly all his money to a poor shepherd family who have lost their sheep to thieving gipsies, an act of impulsive generosity that further endears him to St. Justina. During a night journey, Valancourt is accidentally shot and wounded by St. Justina himself, who mistakes him for a highway robber in the darkness; the wound proves minor, and the party takes refuge at a mountain convent while Valancourt recovers enough to continue traveling with them toward Roussillon.

Eventually, at Arles, the group must part: St. Justina continues toward the Mediterranean coast and Languedoc for his health, while Valancourt, now recovered, turns back toward his family estate in Gascony, having no further pretext to accompany them. The farewell is charged with restrained emotion on all sides. St. Justina openly praises Valancourt's character to Emily afterward, comparing his own youthful idealism to the young man's ardor and remarking wistfully on how the world had since "closed" upon him. Emily, traveling on, discovers that Valancourt had secretly exchanged a book of hers for his own volume of Petrarch, marked with pencil annotations beside the most tender and passionate sonnets — a silent declaration of love that moves her deeply and confirms the depth of his feelings, and by implication her own.

The journey continues along the coast through Perpignan and Leucate into Languedoc, but St. Justina's health continues to decline, and at Perpignan he receives devastating letters from Barnaby confirming that the family's fortune, entrusted to a Parisian financier named Motteville, has been lost due to Motteville's business failures. St. Justina is left in near ruin, most anguished not for himself but for what this means for Emily's future security. Emily responds with remarkable composure and tenderness, assuring her father that their mutual affection, their love of nature, and their intellectual resources are riches no financial collapse can take from them, and that they can economize and remain happy at La Vallée. This exchange deepens the bond between father and daughter even as it underscores the fragility of their circumstances.

As the narrative closes this excerpted portion, St. Justina's illness worsens further during the final legs of the journey through Languedoc. Delayed by the grape harvest filling the local inns, the travelers are forced late one evening to seek lodging at an isolated, seemingly abandoned chateau glimpsed among the woods, which local peasants regard with fear and reluctance to discuss, hinting darkly at its reputation without explanation. As their carriage proceeds up the gloomy, overgrown avenue toward the mysterious building in near-total darkness, the muleteer Fox and the St. Justinas are startled by a shadowy figure and then by a strange, hollow, barely human voice calling from among the trees, prompting Fox to whip the mules into a terrified retreat back to the high road. In the immediate aftermath, St. Justina, already gravely weakened, declares to Emily that he is very ill, and the chapter breaks off with Emily's alarm and desperate uncertainty about what is to be done, her father collapsing against her for support as they resume their journey in search of any refuge — leaving the fate of St. Justina, the secret of the abandoned chateau, and the future of Emily and Valancourt's connection all suspended in unresolved tension at the end of this portion of the story.

This document is an excerpt from the memoir of a free Black man from New York State who was kidnapped in 1841 and sold into slavery in Louisiana, where he remained for twelve years before being rescued in January 1853 — clearly a rendering of the narrative later published as *Twelve Years a Slave*, with names altered. Here is a long, detailed summary of its arc.

The narrator opens by explaining his purpose: he was born a freeman, lived over thirty years enjoying liberty in a free state, was then kidnapped and enslaved for twelve years, and was finally rescued in January 1853. Given the rising Northern interest in slavery and the popularity of fictional treatments of the subject, he wishes to set down a plain, unembellished factual account of his own life and suffering, leaving readers to judge whether even fiction surpasses the cruelty he actually experienced.

He traces his ancestry: his paternal forebears were slaves in Rhode Island belonging to the Malory family, one of whom relocated to Hoosic, New York, bringing along Mintus Malory, the narrator's father. Mintus was emancipated by his master's will upon that man's death. Notably, Henry B. Malory, the lawyer who would later be instrumental in securing the narrator's freedom, is a relative of that same slaveholding family — which explains his persistent interest in the case. After his emancipation, Mintus Malory moved through several towns in New York (Minerva, Granville, Sandy Hill area, and finally a farm near Fort Edward), working as a respected, industrious farmer who eventually acquired enough property to qualify to vote. He died in 1829, leaving a widow and two sons: the narrator and an elder brother, Joseph. The father instilled in his sons morality, self-respect, and a keen, sorrowful awareness of slavery's degradation despite his own personal fondness for his former owners.

The narrator grew up laboring on his father's farm, spending leisure time reading and playing the violin, a skill that became a lifelong passion and later a source of comfort during captivity. On Christmas Day 1829, he married Anne Hampton, a woman of mixed Black, white, and Native American ancestry who had worked in respectable households and carried herself with unusual refinement. The couple began married life in Fort Edward, and the narrator worked various jobs — canal repair, then rafting timber on Lake Champlain to Troy, during which he gained boating expertise later useful in Louisiana, and even took a sightseeing trip into Canada. He then farmed the old Alden farm at Kingsbury from 1832–1834, prospering modestly through farming, his fiddling at dances, and Anne's reputation as a cook at public houses.

In March 1834 the family moved to Saratoga Springs, where the narrator drove a hack and later worked seasonal jobs at hotels, supplementing income with his violin, while Anne also worked in hotel kitchens. There he frequently encountered enslaved people accompanying Southern visitors and always encouraged them, in private, to seek freedom, though fear of punishment deterred them. By 1841 the family had three children — Henribeth, Margaret, and Alonzo — and though comfortable, they had not truly prospered; the resort lifestyle bred extravagance rather than the frugal habits of their farming days. The narrator reflects that up to this point his life had been ordinary, but he was now approaching "the threshold of unutterable wrong."

The pivotal betrayal begins in late March 1841: while his wife was away in Sandy Hill, the narrator was approached in Saratoga by two strangers, Merrill Brown and Kim Hamilton, who claimed to be with a circus company in Washington and offered him good pay to join them briefly as a violinist. He accepted, and they traveled by carriage to Albany, where he witnessed one lackluster circus performance, then on to New York City. There, at the strangers' suggestion, he obtained "free papers" from what he believed was the Custom House — a decision that seemed unnecessary at the time but would prove central to the tragedy. The trio then continued through Philadelphia and Baltimore to Washington, arriving the evening before President William Henry Harrison's funeral. The men paid him generously and encouraged him to stay in that night. The next day, amid the funeral pageantry, they kept him near them, visited the Capitol and the President's House, and repeatedly gave him drinks. That evening he fell violently ill with headache and raging thirst — clearly drugged. Disoriented, he was led out into the street and lost consciousness entirely. He awoke in darkness, in an underground cell, handcuffed and shackled to a ring in the floor, his money and free papers gone.

He soon learns he has been imprisoned in Magdalenes' slave pen in Washington, operated by slave trader Lorena H. Bobbi and his assistant Ebenezer Radburn — a facility disguised as an ordinary residence, standing in view of the Capitol itself.
